# Engineering guide

## Purpose and reading order

The latest working handoff (state, uncommitted work, decisions waiting on the user) is `docs/internal/handoff-*.md` (ignored, local), newest date first. `docs/internal/board.md` (ignored, local) says where each phase of the current plan stands, who does what next (Fable plans and reviews, Opus builds, David merges), and holds the prompt for the next session.

Pathlight puts an interactive architecture explorer beside an AI coding
conversation in tmux. It connects architecture, mapped source files, and observed
agent tool activity without pretending to observe runtime traffic.

Read [project intent](docs/project-intent.md) for the product contract,
[README](README.md) for setup/integration, and
[native viewer](docs/native-viewer.md) for controls and rendering limits.

## Current baseline

- The production default is `src/native-viewer.ts`: native OpenTUI widgets,
  an eased Three orthographic camera, orthogonal thin-line connectors, and a
  responsive, draggable inspector. The user approved this camera and appearance.
- The Three candidate has been promoted. `.cache/three-probe/` and
  `.cache/pre-promotion/` are local historical artifacts, not production sources
  or required build inputs. Do not restore the rejected ScrollBox camera.
- The PNG/image renderer was removed; native is the only renderer.
- Linux/tmux is the verified target. Do not claim macOS or broader terminal
  compatibility without checking it. Connectors, cards and the inspector are drawn by OpenTUI; Three only provides the camera projection (no GPU backend is initialised).

The inspector is docked from 120 columns, below the diagram under 120 columns with 40 rows or more, and an overlay otherwise; under 80 columns the diagram is replaced by a node list. The diagram auto-fits on load and resize until the user pans or zooms.

Preserve the approved camera and visual design during maintenance. Propose
intentional redesigns separately; do not quietly substitute another camera.

## Design principle: informative, not a data dump

Pathlight lets an engineer follow what an AI harness is doing, understand their app, and trust an accurate picture of the code and its architecture, simply and intuitively. Show the few things that matter at a glance and keep the rest one deliberate step away (a key, a section, a command). Every new signal (badges, counts, tags, panels) must justify the space it takes, say nothing when there is nothing to say, and never crowd the line or panel it shares. The sidebar was redesigned on 2026-10-24 (Phase 1, from the Claude Design project): a ranked inspector with the component's name and purpose, then Now (its own recent calls), Connects (one row per relationship) and, on request, Files, with the actions and the question field pinned beneath, plus a status tag in each card's top border and a `now`/`last` line in the header. Phase 2 (2026-10-24) added flow mode: `F` draws a flow (a LikeC4 dynamic view, or an agent-written `*.behavior.c4` state diagram) as numbered steps on the diagram with a step reader in the sidebar, dims cards off the path and shows `≠` where a journey hop has no model relationship (a hop back over a pair an earlier step opened is its answer, `↩`, and repeated hops over one pair are one finding); flows are readings, drawn in the agent color and kept apart from observed activity (`src/flow-view.ts`, data from `src/flows.ts`). Phase 6 (2026-11-11) keeps a drawn map current at the end of each turn (`pathlight refresh`) and lets the agent declare a box before writing it (`plan --new`); a box a reload adds is named on header line 2 and draws itself in. The end-of-turn review (2026-10-26) asks for a decision only when there is one: new dependencies since the last commit that the model lacks (`pathlight diff`), shown in the header and reviewed under `c` with `y`/`n`/`e` (`src/review.ts`, `src/viewer/review-view.ts`); it adds no card and no top-level key. The design pass (2026-11-02) set where things go: header line 1 is where you are (and the journey and step), line 2 the box count and the news line (the agent's live work, follow, the `w` offer), the footer only replies to the person's own keys; one vocabulary on screen (journey, boxes, American spelling); reads shown nowhere live; `t`, `m`, `d` a modal beside the conversation and the talk column only where it is hidden (the viewer zoomed). Do not add sections or lines to this layout unless a feature cannot work without it, and treat anything added now as provisional.

## Contracts to preserve

1. **LikeC4 is authoritative.** Keep its identities, hierarchy and explicit
   `navigateTo` links; keep its arrangement (order, ranks, nesting, which side
   an edge leaves); the spacing and card sizes are Pathlight's (compact fit,
   `src/viewer/compact.ts`). Do not infer navigation from shared elements.
2. **Interaction is native.** Nodes are interactive widgets, not highlights
   over an image. Hit targets must match visible terminal cells, including group
   titles after projection, pan, zoom and resize.
3. **State survives workflows.** Search cancellation and Back restore camera and
   selection. Linked-view navigation stays in one process. Editor return retains
   the diagram and file selection. Activity updates must not move the camera or the selection unless the user turned on follow (`a`, off by default); the user's own selection or camera movement pauses it.
4. **Observation is truthful and isolated.** Bind events to workspace, project,
   source and session. Show only observed tool lifecycle states; never infer
   service traffic, test success, or parent activity from a child's event.
   Only actual active operations pulse; connectors do not imply live traffic.
5. **Recording and viewing are separate.** A bound CLI viewer consumes journals.
   OpenCode recording requires opt-in: `pathlight init` (or `init --global`) writes `record: true` on the plugin entry (the counterpart of the Claude hooks), or one session asks with `live: true`. Like the Claude hooks, `record: true` writes nothing in a workspace without a mapping.
   Automatic recording covers root sessions of the plugin's workspace only; closing a viewer does not stop recording.
   Do not silently enable recording. Claude reports a subagent's tool calls under the conversation's own `session_id`; they are recorded in that journal with the subagent's type as an `agent` label (never its id, prompt or results), shown with that label, and can be hidden with `s`. A label must never make a subagent's call look like the conversation's own, and a call that names no file is not shown as activity. OpenCode child sessions are not recorded yet; when they are, each keeps its own journal with a `parent` link and the viewer merges them under the root at read time, labeled. `--follow` is an explicit viewing choice: it tracks only the single most recently active recorded session and never starts recording. Claude hook installation by `pathlight init` is the Claude opt-in.
6. **Resource ownership is scoped.** Use Effect-returning module functions and
   scoped acquisition/finalization for renderers, polling and processes. Preserve
   signal cancellation, editor process-group cleanup, initialization/draw ordering,
   and readiness only after usable rendering. Zod remains at the OpenCode schema
   boundary; follow existing Effect schema/error conventions elsewhere.
7. **Respect the terminal and filesystem.** Never replace a repurposed pane or
   guess the user's pane from a background service. Ask-about-node types only into the pane `pathlight show` was given (`--parent`), verifies it exists, and sends literal text. The Claude Code pane types nothing: it hands the request to the plugin, which submits it through the host. Validate mapped file paths
   before editing. Treat editor commands and executable LikeC4 configuration as
   trusted-workspace inputs.
8. **Keep activity minimal.** Do not store source contents, tool arguments,
   command strings, results or error text in activity journals. A turn marker records only that a prompt began (never its text), and replay reads the same journal (up to 2048 events per session). For shell commands keep only existing workspace files the command names (state `command`, never read/edit). The talk's conversation is read from the host's own file while it is showing and never copied: the session pointer holds a path, a flag and a time only. Preserve bounded
   queues/history and local-only storage; this is not an audit log.
9. **Everything Pathlight writes into a workspace goes in `.pathlight/`** (`src/layout.ts`): the draft's model and `likec4.config.json`, the file mapping, the overlay of names and notes, and agent-written `*.behavior.c4` flows. Nothing is written loose in the root of someone's repository. Ignored, regenerated state (journals, the out-of-date stamp, overlay keys, the fingerprints `pathlight name` records so `brief --changed` can list just the boxes whose files changed) stays in `.cache/pathlight`. There is no fallback that reads the old root location. A model a person wrote elsewhere stays where it is, but its mapping still lives in `.pathlight/`.

## Development and validation

Dependencies are pinned in `package.json` and `bun.lock`; use Bun. See README
for prerequisites. Full verification needs tmux and Neovim.
Native checks need a working OpenTUI/Three backend but no browser or terminal image protocol. `src/doctor.ts` is `pathlight doctor`; `scripts/build.sh` compiles the single binary, which `tests/binary.test.ts` builds and drives. Anything read from the repository at run time (skills, themes) must be compiled in, because the binary has no checkout beside it.

```sh
bun install
bun run check
TMPDIR=/tmp/opencode bun run test
```

Create the temporary directory first if it is absent. Start with affected tests,
then run the full suite for renderer/lifecycle changes. The terminal tests use
isolated tmux servers. Do not manipulate unrelated user panes or viewers.

Test observable behavior through the real CLI/terminal where feasible. Keep
assertions on exact selected IDs, visible file rows, connector cells, and camera
position—not just footer text that can appear before layout settles. Preserve
coverage for mouse wheel handling separately from keyboard scrolling, and pan
preservation separately from zoom preservation. Avoid test-only production seams.

For a manual check, use a real terminal:

```sh
bun run pathlight view services --workspace examples/parcel --project parcel
```

For a pane beside the user, obtain their actual tmux pane ID and use `show` with
`--pane`; include `--socket` for a non-default server. Exercise both flat and nested
views, wide/narrow layouts, search/Back, editor return and activity isolation.
ANSI reconstructions are useful diagnostics, not screenshots of the user's terminal.

`scripts/ansi2png.py` renders `tmux capture-pane -e -p -N` output to a PNG so appearance changes can be inspected; it approximates your terminal's font.

Screens are kept as text: `tests/golden/*.txt` are what `pathlight see` prints for the frozen fixture at several sizes, and `tests/golden.test.ts` compares them. A change to the diagram, header, footer or inspector fails there with a readable diff; when it is meant, look at the new screen and bless it with `UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 TMPDIR=/tmp/opencode bun test tests/golden.test.ts`. `pathlight see` runs the viewer in a private tmux server, so it never touches the user's panes; it is also how an agent can check what a person would see (`--cols`, `--rows`, `--select ELEMENT`, `--keys`).

Map quality is measured, not judged: see [docs/eval.md](docs/eval.md) for the independent scan comparison (`tests/eval/facts.ts`), the model scorer and the authors' rules (`tests/eval/run.ts`). Any change to the scanner, the draft or the skill should be re-scored. Flows have their own score (`tests/eval/flows.ts`, answers in `tests/eval/references/flows.json`): re-run it after a change to `pathlight flow`, the `d` request or the behavior skill.

Keep README and the native controls document aligned with shipped behavior.
Update project intent when an approved product decision changes, distinguishing
implemented behavior from desired or unverified behavior. Bump `scanRevision` in `src/scan.ts` whenever a scanner change can alter its output for the same files: `pathlight diff` caches the base commit's scan and trusts it only for the same revision.

Do not commit or push
unless the governing session instructions explicitly permit it.

# pathlight behavior

A behavior view answers "what should happen, step by step?" It is a state diagram you write from reading the code, drawn in the same LikeC4 workspace as the architecture and opened with `pathlight show`. The architecture map is scanned from the code; this is not. It is **your reading of the code**, so say so, and never present it as verified.

## Truthfulness

- A behavior view is a claim, not an observation. Every state and transition must come from code you read, and each state names the files it comes from (see below). Do not invent a state to make the picture complete. Leave a gap and say what you could not find.
- Finding a bug means reasoning through the transitions and seeing one that gives the wrong result for the user, or a combination of events nobody handled. Say what you traced and what you did not. A formal checker (TLA+ or another) finds more, but it is optional and you must not assume one is installed.
- Never change product code because a diagram looks wrong unless the user asks. Report the bug in plain words, as the steps that lead to it.

## Where it goes

Write one file per flow in the folder of the LikeC4 project it belongs to (`.pathlight/` for the model `pathlight draft` writes), named `NAME.behavior.c4` (for example `messages.behavior.c4`). `pathlight draft` leaves these alone, so a rerun never loses them. If the project has no model at all, ask before creating `likec4.config.json` and `pathlight.activity.json` in `.pathlight/` (see the map skill, `/pathlight:map`).

Put one flow in one `flow` element, tagged `#behavior`, with its states inside it, and name the flow after what it is (`signup`), because top-level ids are shared with the generated architecture model and a clash stops it compiling. Declare `tag behavior` in the file's `specification`, as the example does: it keeps the flow out of the architecture views. Avoid LikeC4 reserved words as ids (`storage`, `notation`, `model`, `view`, `style`, `group`).

```likec4
specification {
  element flow
  element state
  element decision
  tag behavior
  tag bug
  tag fixed
}
model {
  signup = flow 'Signing up' {
    #behavior
    start = state 'Someone opens the sign-up page' {
      description 'src/web/signup.ts'
    }
    taken = decision 'Is the email already used?'
    error = state 'They see "email taken"' {
      #fixed
      description 'src/web/signup.ts, src/api/users.ts'
    }
    created = state 'Account created, welcome email sent'
    double = state 'Two accounts exist for one email' {
      #bug
      description 'Two requests at once both pass the check. src/api/users.ts'
    }
    start -> taken 'submits the form'
    taken -> error 'yes'
    taken -> created 'no'
    taken -> double 'no, and a second request arrives first'
  }
}
views {
  view signup of signup {
    title 'What happens when someone signs up'
    description 'Agent-written from src/api/users.ts and src/web/signup.ts. Synced at 3f2a9c1.'
    include *
    autoLayout TopBottom
  }
}
```

## How to draw it

1. **States are what the person sees**, in their words ("Your phone buzzes after you opened it"), not function names. A state is a place the flow rests; a `decision` is a question with two or more answers.
2. **Transitions are the events**, written on the arrow as the title ("you walk away without reading it"). One transition per cause. If one cause can lead to two states, draw a decision.
3. **Start from the real code path.** Read the handlers and follow each branch. Draw the ordinary path first, then the unusual ones (retries, two things at once, going offline, an expired session).
4. **Keep it small.** Roughly 8 to 25 boxes. Split a flow that needs more into two views linked with `navigateTo`.
5. **Say where each state lives.** Put the files in its `description`, as the example does. This is how someone reviewing the diagram opens the code.

## Marking findings

- A state the user should not be able to reach, or that gives the wrong result, gets `#bug`. Its description says in one sentence why it happens.
- Once the code is changed and you have read the changed code, add a `#fixed` state next to it showing the corrected outcome, linked from the bug with a transition titled `with the fix`. Leave the `#bug` state in so the history reads.
- No tag means "traced, and it works". It does not mean tested.

pathlight draws `#bug` boxes with a red outline and `#fixed` ones green.

## Journeys: how a request moves through the components

A state diagram says what a person sees. A **journey** says which components a request passes through, in order, and pathlight draws it on the architecture itself. It is a LikeC4 `dynamic view` over components the model already has, one step per hop, each titled with the event.

### Which model traces (hosts where the person has several models)

Claude Code pins the tracer to Sonnet itself, so skip this there. In OpenCode and any host with a `pathlight_models` tool, call it before the first trace. It reports the model the tracer will use and why. If `tracer.source` is `sonnet` or `option`, say which model in one line and carry on. If it is `none`, nothing tested is available to this person: do not pick a model yourself. Show them `usable` (the models they can use, with prices), name at most two that look like a fair step down from their current model for reading code, say that none has been measured for this (only Sonnet-class models have, docs/eval.md), and ask which they want, or to keep their current model. After they answer, set `options.tracerModel` as `provider/model` on the pathlight plugin entry in `opencode.json`, tell them to reload OpenCode, and note the choice in your reply. On a flat-rate plan a cheaper model may save nothing, so "keep my current model" is a real answer.

### Working it out

The story comes from reading the code. If a `pathlight-tracer` agent is available (the Claude plugin ships one, pinned to a mid-size model), hand the whole job to it: give it the component, the question and the files, let it run the steps below and write the journey, then pass on its report, including what it left out and anything `pathlight flows` flagged. Reading ten files is work a large conversation model should not spend its tokens on, and the files stay out of the conversation. Do not hand it to a smaller model than that: a smaller one did not do this reliably in testing. If there is no such agent, do the steps yourself, in this order, and do not skip the second:

1. **Trace the path.** Pick the entry point (a route, a command, a handler, the thing the person clicks). Follow it through the code and list, in order, the files it passes through, which component each belongs to (`pathlight list --workspace .` and the model give the ids) and the call that leads to the next. Hand back facts and file names, no claims about what they mean. `pathlight scan` lists the imports if a map is needed.
2. **Decide.** Open the files yourself: any trace you were handed is a list of leads, not facts. Confirm each hop is really in the code, settle the order and the event on each arrow, and drop any hop you cannot point to in a file. If the code is unclear, leave the hop out and say so. Say where the story and the model disagree: a hop the code makes and the model has no relationship for (the command prints it) means the model may be missing a relationship, so name it for the person, and do not add the relationship yourself to silence the warning.
3. **Write it with the command, not by hand.**

```sh
pathlight flow add place-order --workspace . \
  --title 'Placing an order' \
  --reads src/web/checkout.ts,src/api/checkout.ts \
  --step 'customer -> parcel.storefront: opens checkout' \
  --step 'parcel.storefront -> parcel.commerce.api: submits the cart' \
  --step 'parcel.commerce.api -> parcel.commerce.orders: commits the order @ src/api/checkout.ts#commitOrder'
```

End a step with ` @ file#function` when the hop is a call to an exported function (`commitOrder` above): the file must be one of `--reads` and must export that name, or the command refuses it. It copies the declaration from the file, and the viewer shows the name and signature in the step reader, so the person sees what is called without opening the file. Name the function that does what the step says (the handler that receives the request, the one that polls), not the one that merely creates the object doing it. Give every hop you can; a flow with no function names leaves the reader with only your sentences. Leave it off for a hop you cannot point to a function for; never guess a name.

A hop over HTTP, a websocket or a spawned process is not an import, so the model may have no relationship for it. When you have read both the file and line that make the request (the fetch, the socket send, the spawn) and the file that answers it (the route, the handler, the program run), say so on the step: `--step 'parcel.storefront -> parcel.commerce.api over http: submits the cart'` (`over websocket`, `over process`). The view keeps it in the step's notes, the step reader shows `over http` instead of a gap, and `pathlight flows` does not report it. Without both reads, leave `over` off: the command then reports the hop once as a gap; leave it in and say so. Never add `over` to silence a gap. A step back along the way an earlier step went is read as that step's answer and is not reported.

`pathlight flow add` checks every component against the model (and offers the nearest id when one is mistyped), requires the files you read, stamps the view with the commit, writes `place-order.behavior.c4` (in the folder of the LikeC4 project it is for; pass `--project NAME` when the repository has several), takes the file back out if the model would stop compiling, and prints what `pathlight flows` finds. Use `--force` to replace one it wrote and `pathlight flow remove place-order` to delete it; it never overwrites or removes a file a person or agent wrote by hand. The command writes down your reading; it does not make the reading right.

If you must write the view by hand (for example to combine it with a state diagram in one file), this is the shape:

```likec4
views {
  dynamic view placeorder {
    title 'Placing an order'
    description 'Agent-written from src/web/checkout.ts and src/api/checkout.ts. Synced at 3f2a9c1.'
    customer -> parcel.storefront 'opens checkout'
    parcel.storefront -> parcel.commerce.api 'submits the cart'
    parcel.commerce.api -> parcel.commerce.orders 'commits the order'
  }
}
```

- Put it in the same `*.behavior.c4` file as the state diagram it belongs to, or its own; `pathlight draft` leaves those files alone.
- Every hop should be a relationship the model already has. A hop it does not have is shown with `≠ no arrow on the map for this hop` and listed by `pathlight flows`: that is the story and the model disagreeing, so say which one you think is wrong instead of adding the relationship to make the warning go away.
- Name the files you read in the `description`, and the commit (`Synced at <short sha>`). A journey is your reading of the code, drawn in the agent's color and labeled so; it never says what happened.
- The person traces it with `F` in the viewer (`[` `]` to step, `esc` to leave) and sees which components the agent has touched along it. Mark nothing as passed or failed: observed calls are shown beside the steps and are not part of the flow.

## Keeping it true

- Write the commit you read the code at into the view's `description` (`Synced at <short sha>`), as the example does. Get it with `git rev-parse --short HEAD`.
- Before using or extending a behavior view, run `pathlight flows --workspace .`. It lists, per flow, files a state names that are gone or changed since the sync commit, arrows with no event, decisions with fewer than two answers, states nothing reaches, and states that name no file (those cannot be checked at all); and, per journey, hops the model has no relationship for and components whose files changed since the sync commit. If anything changed, re-read those parts and update the view, and only then move the sync commit forward. A clean report means the diagram has not visibly drifted from the files it names, not that it is right.
- Say plainly when you did not do that: "this diagram was last checked at <sha>".

## Show it

`pathlight show VIEW --workspace . --follow` with the view id (`signup` above). `pathlight list --workspace .` lists every view. The relationship titles (the events) appear in the inspector under Connections when a box is selected; the diagram itself draws no text on arrows, so make each state name read on its own.

# pathlight

pathlight shows a LikeC4 architecture diagram in a tmux pane beside the conversation and lights up the components whose mapped files you read or edit. LikeC4 owns the model; `.pathlight/pathlight.activity.json` maps file globs to element ids.

## Truthfulness

- Say only what the tools reported. A scan or check is **static evidence** (imports in TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go and Rust). It does not show what runs, what is called over a network, or that a test passes.
- Never describe the diagram from memory. Open it, or run `pathlight list`, and report what happened.
- Do not invent elements or relationships to make a check pass. A relationship needs a reason you can state from the code you read.
- The viewer shows only observed tool calls. Never imply traffic between components.

## First run

When the user has just installed pathlight, asks you to set it up, `pathlight list` returns no views, or `pathlight open` says there is no model, run `pathlight setup --workspace .` first. It checks tmux, `pathlight` on the PATH, the model, the file mapping and the Claude plugin, prints what is wrong with the fix for each, and, if there is no model, says what it would write. Show the user that output and ask, naming what `--yes` writes: three new files in a new `.pathlight/` folder (`pathlight.model.c4`, `pathlight.activity.json` and `likec4.config.json`), nothing else in the repository touched. **Then end your turn with that question.** Their yes is the only agreement: a clean repository, a sandbox, a scratch copy or auto mode is never agreement, and neither is the request to map the code. Only after they say yes run `pathlight setup --workspace . --yes`: it draws a first picture from the code, checks it, and prints how to open the viewer. Then **name the boxes** (next section), so the first thing they see is explained, and open it. It never rewrites a model the user wrote, and it leaves hooks and recording to `pathlight init`, which you run only with their agreement. If a step it names needs something you cannot do (installing the binary or the plugin), say so and give them the command it printed.

No views means no model *now*. It is not a question about git: do not run `git status` or `git checkout` to look for an older model, and do not offer to restore deleted model files. If the user removed `pathlight.model.c4` or the other root files on purpose (older versions wrote them there; everything now lives in `.pathlight/`), that is the clean start. Go straight to `pathlight setup`, and mention a stale copy in git only if they ask.

## Commands

Run `pathlight --help` for every flag. If `pathlight` is not on the PATH, ask the user how it is installed (the repository's `bun link`, or `bun <repo>/src/cli.ts`).

- `pathlight list --workspace .` lists the views (id, title, project) as JSON.
- `pathlight show VIEW --workspace . --follow` opens the viewer in the user's tmux window and follows this session. Inside tmux it finds the pane itself; from a background service pass the user's actual pane with `--pane %ID` (and `--socket PATH` for a non-default tmux server). Never guess a pane.
- `pathlight scan --workspace . --out scan.json` writes the static facts: files, imports (with lines), external packages, what could not be resolved, and `coverage`.
- `pathlight check --workspace .` compares the model and mapping with a fresh scan. `--json` gives data; `--strict` exits 1 when anything is found.
- `pathlight refresh --workspace .` is what the end of your turn runs (see **The map keeps itself current**); you do not need to run it yourself.
- `pathlight draft --workspace .` writes a first picture made from the code alone (packages, folders, the imports between them, several views); see the next section. `--out DIR` writes it elsewhere.
- `pathlight setup --workspace .` is the first run (see above); add `--yes` to let it draw a first model.
- `pathlight brief --first-day --workspace .` prints the briefing for a person new to the code (what it is, how it is built, where it starts, the journeys, how sure the names are), derived each time and stored nowhere. `pathlight point ELEMENT --workspace .` asks an open viewer to select one box once (with `--journey ID --step N` it also reads that journey at that step) (the onboarding skill's walk (`/pathlight:onboarding`) uses it, after asking); with no element it clears the mark. A request to point the viewer at something is one `pathlight point` command and one line of reply, with no reading and no file list; when it says no viewer is open, reopen it with `pathlight open --workspace .` (it follows the latest session and finds the pane in tmux) or `pathlight show VIEW --workspace . --follow`, never `show` without `--follow` (an unbound viewer cannot send `m`, `t` or `d` here), say so in that line, and point. When `point` answers that a name is two boxes (one's id and another's key), repeat it with the name it gives for the box you meant, still one line of reply.
- `pathlight brief [KEY ...] --workspace .` lists what an agent needs to name boxes: the files each box owns, what it imports from and what imports it (with what each arrow uses, `calls saveOrder`), what is inside it, any name it has. `pathlight name KEY --title TEXT --note TEXT --workspace .` (or `--from FILE|-` with a JSON array of `{"key","title","note"}`) saves names as the agent's reading and redraws once; it never replaces a name the user wrote.
- `pathlight doctor --workspace .` checks tmux, the model, the file mapping and the plugin and prints the fix for each failure. Run it first when the viewer does not open or nothing is recorded.
- `pathlight init --workspace .` wires Claude Code hooks (`.claude/settings.local.json`, per user), the OpenCode plugin, this skill, and proposes a mapping by matching element names to files on disk. It turns on recording, so tell the user what it will write and get their agreement first. `--no-claude-hooks` skips the project-local hooks when the Claude plugin is installed.

## Show the architecture

1. `pathlight list --workspace .` and pick the overview view.
2. `pathlight show VIEW --workspace . --follow`. If the user named a view (for example `/pathlight:map services`), show that one.
3. Report only whether it opened.

If `list` returns no views the workspace has no model yet: follow **First run** above. Write a model by hand (below) only when the user asks for one instead of the draft; then name the files you would write, in `.pathlight/` (everything pathlight writes goes there, so nothing lands loose in the root), and write nothing until they agree.

## After the draft: name the boxes

A fresh draft shows what the code does, not what it is for: every box is a folder name with a line count. The first run is not finished until the boxes say what they are for, so after `setup --yes` do this (the user has already agreed to the draft; naming only writes `.pathlight/pathlight.overlay.json`, as your reading, and never replaces a name they wrote):

- If you have a `pathlight-namer` agent, hand the whole job to it: "Name every box of the pathlight map in this workspace." It runs on a mid-size model, so the reading stays out of this conversation and off a larger model. Otherwise do it yourself as below.
- Run `pathlight brief --workspace .`. When the map was named before and the user asks to refresh it, run `pathlight brief --changed --workspace .` instead: it lists only boxes that are new or whose files changed since they were named, so only those need reading. Boxes come children first. The files listed are the box: a folder plus a loose file beside it is one box, so describe all of it. Open the files that decide what a box is for (the entry point, the biggest file, a README) and name it for what it does in this app, not what it holds. Say when a note is inferred from file names; never describe behavior you did not see.
- Save a level at a time, one line per batch: `pathlight name --workspace . --from - <<< '[{"key":"...","title":"...","note":"..."},{...}]'` (title up to 60 characters, note up to 300, one line; an apostrophe inside the JSON written `'\''`), never a heredoc, because a heredoc holding JSON is refused under the `Bash(pathlight *)` rule that `init` writes. The key is exactly the one `brief` printed.
- The box that holds the whole app gets a note on what the app is for: `brief` opens with the project's own description and README for it. Name it last.
- The namer replies with the first-day briefing and the journeys it suggests. Do not show that briefing yet: its **Journeys to follow** is still empty, and a briefing that changes a minute later is one the user stops trusting.
- First record the up to three journeys the namer suggested, so the map opens with something to follow: hand each to the `pathlight-tracer` agent (several can run at once; without one, follow the behavior skill (`/pathlight:behavior`) yourself), naming the file it starts at. They are your reading of the code and the viewer labels them so.
- Then run `pathlight brief --first-day --workspace .` once and show it to the user **as printed**, once, whole: paste the command's output in a code block; add nothing above it and cut nothing from it. It needs no summary of your own: it says what the app is, how it is built, where it starts, the journeys and how sure the names are. After it, add what the namer could not tell and which journeys the tracer could not confirm (it drops a hop it cannot point to).
- Then open the viewer. The user presses `F` to step through a journey, and corrects any box with `m` (ask the agent again) or `n` (write it themselves, which becomes a pin).
- Last, offer the walk-through: "Want me to walk you through it?" On yes, follow the onboarding skill (`/pathlight:onboarding`; the briefing, then the journeys step by step with the diagram moving to each step, then one line naming the boxes no journey touched).
- On the first map of a repository, ask once, in one line: "Keep this map current as I work? (yes / only when I ask)". Record the answer with `pathlight config set redraw on --workspace .` (yes) or `pathlight config set redraw off --workspace .` (only when I ask). Unanswered is yes. `pathlight config get redraw --workspace .` prints what was chosen; do not ask again when it prints anything.

## The map keeps itself current

On a map `pathlight draft` drew, the end of each of your turns runs `pathlight refresh`: when files landed where no box claims them, a planned box got its files, or a box's files are gone, it redraws the map, keeping every name. A turn that changed nothing writes nothing. It never redraws a model a person wrote, nor one where redraw is off (then rerun `pathlight draft --workspace .` when asked), and it holds back a redraw that would remove a box a journey uses (`pathlight check` then says which).

When it drew boxes nobody has named, you are sent one line after your turn: "Pathlight drew … new boxes on the map, …, named only by their folders. Hand them to the pathlight-namer subagent with these keys (…)". Do exactly that: give the namer those keys only (without one, `pathlight brief KEY ...` then `pathlight name`, as in **After the draft**), then end your turn with one line on what you named. Do not show a briefing, and do not reply to the line otherwise. It comes once per turn at most.

## A quick draft from the code

When the code already exists and the user wants something to look at straight away, `pathlight draft --workspace .` writes `pathlight.model.c4`, `pathlight.activity.json` and `likec4.config.json` into `.pathlight/` with no judgement involved: each package is a box, top-level folders are components (small folders and loose files share a collection each), and a relationship exists wherever files in one component use code from files in another, titled by what they use (`calls createDocument, presentDocument`) or the import count. A pair that only shares types draws no arrow (it is in the model tagged `#types` and in no view). It also writes views for the landscape, the inside of each package, each component's neighborhood, and import cycles. Every name is a folder or file name and every description is a count. Say that plainly: it shows what the code does, not what it is for.

It never rewrites a model the user wrote (use `--out DIR`), and what it writes is generated: rerun it instead of editing those files by hand. To give a draft better names or a note on what a part is for, write `.pathlight/pathlight.overlay.json` next to it and rerun `pathlight draft`: `{"version":1,"elements":{"packages/core/src/session":{"title":"Sessions","note":"Runs one conversation turn"}}}`. Keys are what the code is (a package directory, a folder path, a file path, or `<directory>#small` / `<directory>#loose` for a collection), not the generated ids, so a name survives when an id moves. A title is at most 60 characters and a note 300; only read the code you are naming. Keys that match nothing are listed after the run: fix or remove them. The overlay can also correct structure: `"merges":[{"title":"Data store","keys":["<folder path>","<folder path>"],"by":"agent"}]` (several folders are one component), `"splits":[{"key":"<folder path>","by":"agent"}]` (a folder opens into a box of its own with one component per subfolder, as the draft opens a big one) and `"relationships":[{"from":"<key>","to":"<key>","title":"reads and writes rows","by":"agent"}]` (a label for an arrow imports already support). Mark what you add `"by":"agent"`. Never change or remove an entry marked `"by":"human"`: those are the user's decisions, and `draft` reports one that differs from the last commit. Propose a merge, split or title only for something you checked in the code. An entry that contradicts the code is skipped and listed after the run, so read that list and fix or drop those entries. The overlay never adds files or invents an arrow. If the user wants different groupings, write a model yourself as below.

## Draft a model for a codebase that has none

Aim for a diagram a person can read in one glance. Build it in levels: a few groups (3 to 7) that say what the code is for, and inside each group its parts. A flat row of 14 boxes is not a readable diagram. A small codebase gives a small diagram; do not pad it. Give every group its own view that opens it up, and link the overview to each: in the overview write `include camenae.web with { navigateTo web }` so the group opens its view (Enter in the viewer).

1. **Scan.** `pathlight scan --workspace . --out scan.json`. Read `coverage` first: `unscanned` lists languages the scan does not read (their dependencies are missing, so read those parts of the code yourself), and `unresolved` lists imports it could not follow.
2. **Find the boundaries.** Use the import edges to see which files belong together and which depend on which. Read a few entry points and the files at the center of the graph; do not read everything. Filename families (`chat-*`, `auth-*`), package directories and `external` packages are all hints, not answers.
3. **Write the model.** Use `.c4` files with a `likec4.config.json`, in `.pathlight/`. The syntax you need is under "LikeC4 in brief" below. Give each element a title, technology and a one-sentence description taken from code you read. Name each relationship for what the dependency is ("Reads the model"), not for something you did not see. A relationship on a group is supported by imports between its children. Do not install or run `likec4`: `pathlight check` loads the model itself and fails with "Invalid LikeC4 model" and the parser errors if it is wrong, so a clean check also means the model is valid.
4. **Write `.pathlight/pathlight.activity.json`.** `{ "version": 1, "project": "<likec4 project name>", "mappings": [{ "glob": "src/auth/**", "element": "<exact element id>" }], "ignore": ["tests/**"] }`. Globs are workspace-relative. Element ids are the full dotted ids (`backend.auth`). Use `ignore` for tests, vendored or generated code that is deliberately outside the model.
5. **Check, then adjust.** `pathlight check --workspace .` and work through it:
   - *glob matches no files*: fix the glob.
   - *source files map to no element*: map them, or add them to `ignore` if they are deliberately outside the model.
   - *no import between the mapped files*: the relationship may really run through a network call, an event or a file. Keep it if you can say how; otherwise remove it. Either import direction counts as evidence.
   - *imports with no relationship*: add a relationship when the dependency matters at this level; leave small shared helpers alone.
   - *not checkable*: an end has no mapped files; map it or accept that nothing can be checked.
   - *views with no navigateTo pointing to them*: a diagram has one entry, the overview. Link the others from it, as above.
   - *an element has many elements side by side*: group related ones under a parent and give each group its own view (see below). Do not leave more than about 7 elements at one level.
   - *an element holds many of the mapped files*: the report lists the folders inside it. Split it along them if they are different parts of the system; otherwise leave it and say so.
   - *resources* (databases, queues, third-party APIs: the elements under `"resources"` in `.pathlight/pathlight.activity.json`, each with the packages that lead to it): an arrow to one is checked by its source's imports of those packages. *No file imports … any more* means the code stopped using it; remove the element or ask the user. An import of its package with no arrow is listed with the other imports with no relationship: add the arrow. *Declared in … ; no code imports it* is a box only a compose file runs: say so in your report and leave it; it is not a mistake. A repository with only infrastructure (Helm charts, compose files, Terraform) and no code the scan reads is drafted as one view, `index`, of those boxes and no arrows: say that is what it shows. When infrastructure defines more programs than there are code files, each Helm workload and compose service is a `container` box (inside a box for its chart or compose file) with arrows to the resources its files name (`secret …`, `depends_on …`, an environment name); `check` judges those arrows by the files (*its infrastructure no longer names it*), and the mapping lists them under `"programs"`. Name a program from its template or image (`pathlight brief` lists its key, `program:<file>#<name>`). In a model you write, give a resource its own element with its kind as a tag (`#database`, `#queue`) and list it there.
   - *shared types and utilities that everything imports*: list the element in `"shared": ["<element id>"]` in `.pathlight/pathlight.activity.json`, so `check` stops asking for a relationship to it. Only do this for code that is genuinely used everywhere.
   - *two elements import each other* (`check` says "both ways"): draw one relationship in the direction the stronger dependency runs, say in its description that the other direction exists, and do not hide it by moving files unless the user asked for a restructure.
   - *one file does two jobs*: put it with the element that most of its importers belong to, and name the second job in that element's description.
   - *the model needs `specification` kinds*: declare the element kinds you use once, in a `specification` block (a separate `spec.c4` is fine).
6. **Show it** with `pathlight show`.
7. **Report plainly**, every time and without being asked, as this checklist (say "none" rather than leaving an item out):
   - what the scan covered: files, imports, and anything under `unscanned` or `unresolved` (languages or imports it could not read);
   - what the model contains: elements, and the views you made;
   - what was left out: the "N source files ignored on purpose" line and the kinds of file in `ignore` (tests, tooling, examples), so they can decide whether any belongs in the diagram;
   - what `check` could not verify: relationships marked "not checkable", and relationships you kept with no import behind them, each with the reason you kept it.

## LikeC4 in brief

This is the whole of the syntax a pathlight model needs; the example is compiled by a test, so copy its shape. Anything beyond it is on https://likec4.dev/dsl/, and `pathlight check` reports a mistake with the parser's message.

```likec4
specification {
  element system
  element component
  tag planned
}
model {
  app = system 'Orders' {
    description 'Takes and fulfils orders.'
    api = component 'Order API' {
      technology 'Express'
      description 'Validates an order and stores it.'
    }
    store = component 'Order store' {
      #planned
      technology 'Postgres'
    }
    api -> store 'Writes orders'
  }
  billing = system 'Billing'
  app.api -> billing 'Asks it to charge the customer'
}
views {
  view index {
    title 'Overview'
    include app with { navigateTo app }
    include billing
  }
  view app of app {
    title 'Inside Orders'
    include *
    autoLayout LeftRight
  }
}
```

- **Kinds** (`system`, `component`) are declared once in `specification`; a tag is declared there as `tag name` and used as `#name`.
- **An element** is `id = kind 'Title' { ... }` with optional `technology`, `description` and nested elements. Its relationships go inside the parent (`api -> store 'label'`) or anywhere with full dotted ids (`app.api -> billing`).
- **Ids** are letters, digits, `_` and `-`, not starting with a digit. A dot is the path separator (`app.api`), never part of an id. Avoid reserved words as ids (`storage`, `notation`, `model`, `view`, `style`, `group`).
- **A view** is `view name { ... }`, or `view name of element { ... }` to open one element up. `include *` is the element's children (or the top level in a view with no `of`); `include a.*` is the children of `a`; `include a, b` lists elements; `exclude` removes. `*` only works alone or after a dot: there is no pattern such as `signup_*`.
- **Linking views:** `include app with { navigateTo app }` makes the box open view `app` (Enter in the viewer). Every view except the overview should be linked from it.
- **Quotes:** single or double; put a long text on its own lines inside `'''` triple quotes only if you need line breaks.
- **Several files** in one folder with one `likec4.config.json` (`{"name": "demo"}`) form one model; across files an element is referenced by its full dotted id.

## Design the architecture before the code exists

When there is little or no code yet, the model is the plan, and writing it with the user is the work. Agree the components and relationships with them, write the model, and map each component to the files you expect to create. Then list the components that do not exist yet in `"planned": ["<element id>", ...]` in `.pathlight/pathlight.activity.json` (an element covers everything inside it). `pathlight check` then reports the plan and how much of it exists instead of calling those globs mistakes, and the viewer draws unbuilt ones dashed with a `[planned]` tag.

As files appear, `check` says "<id> now has files: remove it from planned"; do that. From then on its relationships are checked against the code, so a relationship the plan drew that the code does not have is reported as unsupported: that is the plan and the code disagreeing, and the user decides which to change. Never add an element to `planned` to hide a glob that is simply wrong.

On a large codebase do not stop at one flat diagram. Make an overview, then a view for each component that has several parts inside, and say which parts you did not open up. A draft opens a folder that is most of its package on its own, with a view of its subfolders; to open another, add a `split` for it to the overlay.

When you create, move or delete files later in the session, add or fix their mapping in `.pathlight/pathlight.activity.json` in the same change, so the viewer lights the right component instead of listing the file as `no component`.

Run `pathlight check` again after any later change to the code or the model, and report what it says without softening it.

## Say where you are about to work

Before a change that spans several parts, run `pathlight plan <element id> [...]` with the ids from the model you expect to touch (ids only, no text), and `pathlight plan` with none when you finish. The viewer outlines those elements in purple and marks activity on any other element `off plan`, so the user sees at once when the work wandered. Unknown ids are refused. It is a statement of intent, not a record: if the plan turns out wrong, set a new one. A plan from an earlier session is not shown.

## Requests from the viewer

The person points at a box and presses `t` to ask how something works or to tell you what to change; the request arrives here as one line, `About the "<title>" component (<id>): <their words> [files: …; connects: …]`, followed by what to do with it. The files it names are the ones on the box's edges, not all of them.

- **A question whose answer is a path** (the line asks you to record it as a pathlight journey): answer here in chat, then have the path recorded with `pathlight flow add`, so it appears on the map and they press `F` to walk it. If you have a `pathlight-tracer` agent, hand the recording to it with the component, their question and the files: it runs on a mid-size model, so the reading stays out of this conversation and off a larger model. Otherwise follow the behavior skill (`/pathlight:behavior`) yourself. The same goes for a request from `d` ("Trace how this works in … and record it as a pathlight journey"): pass that line to the tracer as it is. Say which hops it could not confirm.
- **An instruction** (add, change, move, remove, rename: anything that will edit files): before you touch a file, run `pathlight plan <id> [...]` with the box they pointed at and every other element the change will reach, so the outline appears where they pointed before the first edit lights it; `pathlight plan` with no ids when you are done. For a part that does not exist yet, declare it first so the person sees it appear where it will go. On a drafted map (its `pathlight.model.c4` starts with "Generated by `pathlight draft`"), which is most maps: `pathlight plan --new internal/auth --title "Auth middleware" --note "Checks the session before any handler runs." [other ids ...] --workspace .`, with the folder you are about to create beside the folders that are boxes. It draws a dashed box with that name, sets the plan to it and the ids you give, and refuses a folder inside another box (name the folder one level up) or one that already has files (plan its id instead). When its files exist the end of your turn makes it solid, with its arrows, and keeps the name; you do not rerun `draft`. If you end up not building it, take it back with `pathlight plan --drop internal/auth --workspace .` before the turn ends. On a model a person wrote, add the element to the model, map the files you will create in `.pathlight/pathlight.activity.json` and list its id under `"planned"` there (see **Design the architecture before the code exists**). Declare only what you will build this turn, and draw no arrow the code does not have yet: a journey (`pathlight flow add`) is where an intended path goes.
- **An improve-the-map request** (`m`, "Improve the pathlight map for …"): a change you advise against (a merge, a split, a rename) is proposed with your reasons and not replaced by a different change; rename or redraw nothing until the person says yes.

A hop you confirmed over HTTP, a websocket or a spawned process, which no import backs, is recorded as such: `--step 'app -> server over http: opens the document'` (`over websocket`, `over process`). Use it only when the file and line that make the request and the file that answers it have both been read; never to silence a gap.

At the end of a turn the person may review new dependencies in the viewer (`c`). A request that starts "I reviewed the architecture change" is their verdict: take a rejected dependency out (or say what bigger change that needs and wait), or add an accepted one to a model they wrote, then run `pathlight check`.

## What changed since the last commit

`pathlight diff --workspace .` lists the model's relationships that an import backs now and did not at `HEAD` (or `--base REV`), the ones that lost their imports, and new pairs of elements that import each other with no relationship. Use it before reporting a change that touched structure: an added import between two elements is either a missing relationship to declare or a dependency to question. It is static imports only; say so.

## Keep the model honest

When files are added, moved or removed, run `pathlight check --workspace .` and tell the user what changed: new unmapped files, globs that no longer match, new imports between components. Propose the edits to the model or mapping; do not change the model silently.

## Limits

- The scan reads TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go and Rust. Code in other languages is drawn in its own boxes ("not read by the scan") with no arrows, because its imports are unknown; say so when you describe the map. It does not follow `tsconfig` `extends`, bundler aliases, Python `sys.path` edits, Go build tags or Rust `cfg` (every module is read, `#[cfg(test)]` code is left out); what it cannot resolve is listed, not guessed.
- The viewer is for Linux with tmux. Do not claim other terminals or platforms work.
- Activity journals hold metadata only (tool, operation, file paths, time). Do not add source, commands or results to them.

# pathlight onboarding

A person new to this code wants to know what it is, how it is built and where it starts, and then to follow something through it. The map already holds the facts (the scan, the boxes, the imports) and the agent's reading (names, notes, journeys). This skill gives them those, in that order, and walks the journeys with the diagram beside the chat, one step at a time. A box no journey reaches is a room nobody uses yet: the walk names it at the end and does not tour it.

## The rules of the walk

- **Facts first.** Start from what pathlight prints: `pathlight brief --first-day`, `pathlight brief KEY` for the box in hand, `pathlight flows --json` for a journey's steps. Do not read the code to repeat what these already say.
- **Files second, and narrowly.** When a step needs more, open the one file that decides it (the file the step names, the entry point, the box's largest file) and say which file you read. Never read a whole folder to sound thorough.
- **Cite identifiers.** Name each box with its title and key (`Backend API and services [mealie]`), each file as `path:line`. A sentence about behavior points at where it is.
- **Say what was read and what was inferred.** A note marked `(inferred)` was worked out from file names; say so when you rely on it. Never describe behavior you did not see in code or in a recorded step.
- **Change nothing.** Names come only through the `pathlight-namer` agent and journeys only through the `pathlight-tracer` agent; do not edit the model, the overlay, the mapping or the code.
- The person can stop at any step. Keep each message short: one box or one step, then wait.
- **A long message scrambles the terminal and is not read.** A walk step is at most eight lines: the box as `<title> [<key>]`, what happens here in two or three sentences, one file as `path:line`, and one line on what you did not read; everything else only if asked.

## Before the walk

1. `pathlight list --workspace .`. No views means no map: follow the map skill's **First run** (`/pathlight:map`) (it asks before writing anything), then come back.
2. `pathlight brief --first-day --workspace .`. If most boxes say `not named yet`, the walk would be folder names: say so and offer to have the `pathlight-namer` agent name them first ("Name every box of the pathlight map in this workspace"). A map a person wrote by hand has no drafted boxes; walk its overview view instead, from its own `.c4` files.

## 1. The briefing

Show the output of `pathlight brief --first-day --workspace .` **as printed**: paste the command's output whole, in a code block; add nothing above it and cut nothing from it. When the briefing was already shown in this conversation (the first run ends with it), say "the briefing above" and do not print it again. It already says what it is, how it is built, where it starts, the journeys and how sure the names are. Who owns which part (git history) is not covered; say so if asked.

## 2. Ask once before moving the diagram

"I can move the diagram to each box as we go (it selects the box once and marks it `← agent`; your next key takes over). Shall I?" This is the only question before the walk: take the first journey the briefing lists, never ask "which journey?". Only after a yes, use `pathlight point`. When it answers that no viewer is open, reopen it with `pathlight open --workspace .` (it follows the latest session and finds the pane beside you in tmux), or `pathlight show VIEW --workspace . --follow`, never `show` without `--follow`: an unbound viewer cannot send `m`, `t` or `d` to this conversation. Say so in one line, then point again. When `point` answers that a name is two boxes (one's id and another's key), point again with the name it gives for the box you meant. Say once that they can press `F` in the viewer instead and step through a journey themselves.

## 3. Walk a journey, step by step

A newcomer learns a codebase by following one thing through. Take the first journey the briefing lists, then the next ones if they want them.

- `pathlight flows --json --workspace .` gives each journey's steps: the two components of each hop (`from`, `to`), the step's text, and the function it calls when the tracer recorded one (`call`).
- A hop reads as the viewer's Steps card draws it, `from → to`: `from` is the box whose code acts, `to` is the box it reaches. The diagram's numbers and the pointer follow the arrival (`to`).
- For each step: `pathlight point <to-component> --journey <journey id> --step <n> --workspace .` (the journey's id and the step's number from `pathlight flows --json`), which turns the viewer's journey reading on at that step, the hop drawn and the step reader beside it; then one message of at most eight lines that opens "From <from title>, reaching <to title>": what happens on the hop in two or three sentences (the step's own text, and the boxes' notes from `pathlight brief ID --workspace .`, which takes a step's ids as they are, so there is no key to look up), and the one file the step names, read narrowly and cited as `path:line`: it is the code that acts, so it lives in `from`; then one line on what you did not read.
- A step marked `≠` (no arrow on the map for this hop) is the story and the map disagreeing; say so plainly rather than explaining it away.

**No journey recorded.** Say so. Ask whether the tracer should draw the first journey from the entry point the briefing lists first; on yes, hand it to the `pathlight-tracer` agent with the request the viewer's `d` key sends: `Trace how this works in the "<title>" component (<id>) and record it as a pathlight journey: <what happens from that entry point>`. The tracer decides the journey, never this skill. Without one, go straight to the ending.

## 4. The ending

After the last journey they want, one message:

- one line naming the boxes no journey touched, titles only, in the briefing's order (`Not on any journey: Docs site scripts, Code generators, …`), with no message per box;
- the journeys not walked, by title;
- three questions worth asking with `t` in the viewer, each about a real box or step you showed ("how does Backend API and services check a login?");
- last, when a journey was walked, one line: "The viewer is still reading <journey title>; `esc` there leaves it, `F` opens the next."

Then `pathlight point --workspace .` with no element, to clear the mark.

## A point request

"Point the viewer at …" is one `pathlight point` command and one line of reply ("Pointed at `<title> [<key>]`."): no reading, no file list, no offer. When no viewer is open, reopen it with `pathlight open --workspace .` or `pathlight show VIEW --workspace . --follow` (never without `--follow`), say so in the same line, and point. When `point` answers that the name is two boxes (one's id and another's key), repeat it with the name it gives for the box you meant; the reply is still one line.

## A worked example (`examples/parcel`)

Parcel is a small fictional shop, a map a person wrote: no code, so no journey can be recorded and the briefing has no drafted boxes.

1. `pathlight list --workspace examples/parcel` → views `index`, `services`, `checkout`. The briefing says `no drafted map`, so what it is and how it is built are read from `examples/parcel/model.c4` and `views.c4`.
2. "Parcel is drawn in three views; the overview, *Parcel / System context*, shows the Customer, Parcel itself, and three outside systems: the Payment provider, the Shipping carrier and the Email provider. Shall I move the diagram as we go?" They say yes.
3. "There is no recorded journey, and Parcel has no code to trace one from, so there is nothing to walk yet."
4. The ending: "Not on any journey: Parcel, Storefront, Commerce, Fulfillment, Payment provider, Shipping carrier, Email provider. Worth asking with `t`: how does the Checkout API reach the Payment provider? What does the Outbox relay send, and to whom? Where is stock reserved?" No journey was walked, so the viewer is reading none and there is no `esc` line. Then `pathlight point --workspace examples/parcel` to clear the mark.

On a drafted map the same walk starts from the briefing, walks its journeys step by step, and ends the same way.

# Pathlight

Show LikeC4 architecture diagrams beside an agent conversation in tmux.
LikeC4 owns the model and its arrangement; Pathlight sets the spacing and card sizes so titles stay readable. OpenTUI renders interactive terminal nodes, groups, and connectors by default.
The viewer can show live tool activity mapped to architecture elements. It does not infer test status or runtime service traffic.

See [project intent](docs/project-intent.md) for the goals, accepted design and
scope boundaries, and [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) for engineering guidance.

## Set up

Use Bun 1.4.2 or later, Node.js 22 or later and tmux. `bun run build` compiles one self-contained `dist/pathlight-OS-ARCH` file (verified on Linux x64 only); `pathlight doctor` checks tmux, the model, the file mapping and the plugin, and says how to fix each failure.
The OpenCode plugin targets V2 and is pinned to SDK 2.0.31.

```sh
bun install
```

Native mode needs no browser, GPU backend or terminal image protocol.
Only open trusted LikeC4 workspaces. LikeC4 can load executable JavaScript or TypeScript project configuration.

## Install

Install the `pathlight` command (needs tmux; verified on Linux x64, and the macOS builds the release publishes have not been tried), with npm or the install script:

```sh
npm i -g @dumbbunnyio/pathlight     # npm i -g pathlight installs the same
# or
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dumbbunnyio/pathlight/main/install.sh | sh
```

Then add it to your agent once, for every project.

Claude Code:

```sh
claude plugin marketplace add dumbbunnyio/pathlight
claude plugin install pathlight@pathlight
```

OpenCode:

```sh
pathlight init --global
```

`init --global` adds the `@dumbbunnyio/pathlight-opencode` plugin to OpenCode's own `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` with recording on (the same line you could add yourself: `{ "package": "@dumbbunnyio/pathlight-opencode", "options": { "record": true } }` in `"plugins"`). Like the Claude plugin, it records only in projects that have a map. Restart OpenCode after adding it.

Then, in a project, type `/pathlight:map` in Claude Code or `/pathlight` in OpenCode (or run `pathlight setup --yes`), and `pathlight doctor` if anything is missing. Other agents (Codex, Pi, …) have no plugin yet: the map, the viewer and `check`/`diff` work beside any of them, but the viewer cannot see what they touch.

From a checkout instead: `bun install && bun link`, then `claude plugin marketplace add /path/to/pathlight`.

## Claude Code plugin

The plugin adds the recording hooks and the `/pathlight` skill. Hooks do nothing in a project without `.pathlight/pathlight.activity.json`, so enabling the plugin globally is safe. Create the mapping with `pathlight init --workspace . --no-claude-hooks` (the flag keeps `init` from also writing project-local hooks, which would record every event twice).
Use either this route or the project-local route below, not both.

## First run

In the project you work in, with `pathlight` on your PATH and (for Claude Code) the plugin installed:

```sh
pathlight setup            # checks tmux, the PATH, the model, the file mapping and the plugin; says what it would write
pathlight setup --yes      # with no model yet, draws a first one from the code's imports, checks it, says how to open it
```

Or type `/pathlight:map` in Claude Code (`/pathlight` in OpenCode) and let the agent run both for you, asking first. `setup` writes nothing without `--yes`, never rewrites a model you wrote, and leaves the hooks and recording to `pathlight init` (below), because those change your settings.

The first run ends with a briefing, not just a picture: once the boxes are named, the agent shows `pathlight brief --first-day` as printed (what the app is, how it is built, where the project declares it starts, the journeys to follow with `F`, and how many names were read in the code or only inferred from file names), records the journeys the namer suggested, and offers to walk you through it. The walk is the onboarding skill (`/pathlight:onboarding`, "walk me through this codebase", "onboard me"): the recorded journeys step by step, citing boxes by key and files by line, then one line naming the boxes no journey touched and three questions worth asking with `t`. With your yes it moves the diagram to each step with `pathlight point … --journey ID --step N`, which turns the journey's reading on at that step (the box selected once and marked `← agent` until your next key, the journey until `esc` or the next pointer; it never follows the agent). The briefing is derived each time from the scan, the names and the journeys; nothing new is stored, and Pathlight calls no model: the agent reads, the viewer only points.

## Quick start (Claude Code and OpenCode)

The viewer on one screen, the three keys to start and the rest in three tiers: [docs/quick-start.md](docs/quick-start.md). [The viewer reference](docs/native-viewer.md) has every key.

From the project you work in, after `pathlight setup --yes` has drawn a model (or with one you wrote):

```sh
pathlight init --workspace .
```

`init` adds the Claude Code hooks to `.claude/settings.local.json` (per-user), copies the three pathlight skills as `pathlight-map`, `pathlight-behavior` and `pathlight-onboarding` (the Claude plugin gives them as `/pathlight:map`, `/pathlight:behavior` and `/pathlight:onboarding`),
registers the OpenCode plugin (the `@dumbbunnyio/pathlight-opencode` npm package; from a checkout, its `plugins/opencode` folder), and creates `.pathlight/pathlight.activity.json` if absent and there is a model to map (with none, it says to run `pathlight setup --yes`). It maps only elements whose name matches
a directory or file that exists; review it and add globs for the rest. Re-running `init` is safe and never overwrites an existing mapping.

To reopen the viewer yourself, with no agent involved:

| Where you are | Command | Result | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A shell prompt in a tmux pane | `pathlight open [VIEW]` | That pane becomes the viewer | none |
| Inside Claude Code | `/pathlight:open [tmux\|pane] [VIEW]` | A viewer pane is split beside the conversation, bound to it; with `pane`, or a saved `pane` choice, Pathlight is drawn in Claude Code's own pane instead, which is experimental ([Inside Claude Code](#inside-claude-code)) | none (the plugin answers the command itself, so the model is never called) |
| Inside OpenCode | `/pathlight-open [VIEW]` | A viewer pane is split beside the conversation | none (the CLI plugin handles it) |
| Inside Claude Code or OpenCode | `! pathlight open [VIEW]` | The same split | none (a shell escape) |

`open` follows the most recent recorded session and shows `VIEW`, else the view named `index`, else the first view. Typed at a prompt it takes over that pane; run by an agent (anything between the pane's shell and the command) it splits beside it. `--here` always uses the current terminal and `--split` always splits. Without a `.pathlight/pathlight.activity.json` it still opens, but cannot follow an agent. The hook needs the Claude plugin; `/pathlight:open` is not installed by `pathlight init`.

Then, in tmux, run `/pathlight:map` in Claude Code (or `/pathlight:map VIEW_ID`). The viewer opens beside the conversation and
follows the most recently active recorded session with `--follow`, so you need no pane or session IDs. You can also run it yourself:

```sh
bun run pathlight show VIEW --workspace /path/to/project --follow
```

Installing the Claude hooks is the opt-in for Claude recording; remove them to stop. For OpenCode the opt-in is `record: true` on the plugin entry (what `init` writes) or a `live: true` request.
`--follow` only reads journals: it never starts recording, and it switches to whichever recorded session wrote last. A Claude subagent's calls share the conversation's session and carry a label; OpenCode child sessions are not recorded.
The header shows `● live` (a spinner while a tool runs; the session's id is in `c`), the right of its second row is the news line (the call running now, `now ■ edit in Auth service`, gone once it ends; `following <box>  a stop` while follow is on; or the `w` offer), and the Work card in the inspector lists the selected component's recent edits and commands with their age. Reads are kept for `c` and replay and shown nowhere live. The footer only answers the keys you press; nothing the agent does is reported there.
Boxes show `e`/`c` counts of retained edits and commands. Press `t` to ask the agent about the selected box or tell it what to change. Beside the conversation (the tmux split `pathlight show` opens, or Claude Code's pane) this opens a modal: the kind of request, the box, and a field showing a suggested question (`how does <box> work?`) as ghost text that `→` takes; Enter sends it with the box's context and the reply lands in the conversation beside you. When the conversation is hidden (zoom the viewer's tmux pane, `prefix z`), the inspector's column turns into the talk instead: the conversation of the bound session (your prompts and the agent's text, read from the host's own conversation file and never copied), with a field under it. The first request is typed into your agent's pane with the files on the component's edges and its connections; later ones are your text alone. Enter sends and submits (an empty field sends nothing; `→` takes the suggestion), Alt+Enter adds a line, `z` widens the talk, `i` flips back to the node, Esc steps back. The reply shows in the talk as it arrives, with `⠋ working` under your request, `waiting for you in its pane` (a permission prompt or a question, answered in the agent's pane) or `done`; nothing on the diagram moves. Zooming or unzooming with a request open carries it across. A how-question (the talk says `records a journey` under its tabs) is answered in chat and recorded as a journey that `F` walks; an instruction is declared with `pathlight plan` before the first edit, so the boxes it will touch are outlined first. Press `d` to ask the agent to trace how something works from that box and record it as a journey (it reads the code and runs `pathlight flow add`, in the Claude plugin's Sonnet-sized `pathlight-tracer` agent so the reading does not run on your larger model; `F` shows it once written). Press `m` to ask the agent to improve the map for that box (it reads the files, answers, and proposes a new name, note, merge or split, writing it to the overlay only after your yes) or `n` to name and describe it yourself; both need a map made by `pathlight draft`. Press `1`–`4` to focus an inspector card (Work, Connects or Steps, Files, In journeys; `e` shows the files), `F` to step through a journey on the diagram (the header's first line names the journey, the step and its box), `/` to search every view, box, journey and mapped file (this view's first, exact matches before all; `tab` narrows the list to one kind) and `g` to jump to a view, and `T` to choose a theme (OpenCode-format JSON themes, previewed live). Press `w` to select the node the agent is working on; when that work is in a component this view does not show and the agent's turn is still open, the header says "working in VIEW" beside a highlighted `w` ("go and follow"), once (after `w` and Back it returns only for a later call in another box, or a new turn); once the turn has ended the offer is gone, and `w` goes there and turns follow on (a view this one links to with `navigateTo` first, else the smallest view containing it), never on its own (or click its row in the activity list), and `c` to review the session: new dependencies the code gained since the last commit that the model does not have, each to accept (`y`) or reject (`n`, which asks the agent to take it out), then what the session touched (see [native viewer](docs/native-viewer.md#review-new-dependencies)). Press `a` to follow the work: the viewer selects the box of the newest edit or command, running or finished, and glides the camera to it. Only work that happens after you turn it on (or resume it) counts; `w` jumps to the last work done. It is off by default; while on, it goes to another view when that is where the work is (`b` comes back), and it pauses when you select, pan or zoom (`a` resumes). Calls made inside a Claude subagent are recorded with its type (never its id or prompt) and shown with that label, for example `·Explore`; they land in the same journal as the conversation's own calls. Press `s` to hide or show them.

Press `p` to replay the session: the viewer steps through the recorded calls in order, one call per step, with the component of each step selected and the counts building up as they did. `←`/`→` step, `[`/`]` jump between turns (a turn is one prompt and the work after it), `space` plays and pauses, `s` sets the speed, `esc` returns to live. Replay covers what the journal retained (the last 2048 events of a session) and only the calls, never the prompts.

## Open a diagram

Inside tmux, list the example diagrams, then show one:

```sh
bun run pathlight list --workspace examples/parcel
bun run pathlight show services --workspace examples/parcel
```

Select nodes with the mouse or `h` `j` `k` `l`, which move to the nearest node in that direction. Arrow keys pan the Three camera (press `v` to swap the two). Tab moves into the inspector and through its cards (in a flow it steps). Connections are orthogonal thin lines with rounded bends. Press `/` to search every view, box, journey and mapped file; `tab` narrows the list to one kind (views, boxes, journeys, files), and choosing a journey reads it on the diagram.
The selected node's connections are solid, cyan for incoming and amber for outgoing; the rest are dotted. Focus Connects (its number, or `tab`) and move the cursor onto a row to read a long relationship in full. Its last rows, muted, say `types only`: boxes this one shares only types with, which a drafted map does not draw.
Press `e` to browse the selected node's mapped files, then Enter to open one in your external editor (at its first uncommitted change, if it has one).
Set `VISUAL` or `EDITOR` before starting the viewer. File browsing does not require live recording.
Enter goes into a box: into its children when this view draws them (a group, or the frame the view is about), else into the view it opens; `o` opens that view even when the children are drawn here, and the inspector says `o opens VIEW` only then. `b` and Backspace step back through the views and selections you visited; with nowhere to go back to, Backspace goes up to the parent group, then to the view that opens this one.
Use `f` to fit, `r` to center the selection, and `q` to quit. Press `i` to show or hide the inspector (docked from 120 columns, below the diagram under 120 columns with 40 rows or more, an overlay otherwise; under 80 columns the nodes are a list) or `?` for help. The diagram refits on resize until you pan or zoom; `f` fits again. Set `PATHLIGHT_COLORS=256` if your terminal lacks 24-bit color and is not detected. Ctrl+C quits even while search is active.

To run in the current terminal instead of opening a pane:

## Scan a codebase

`pathlight scan --workspace . --out scan.json` reads the TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go and Rust source statically (the parsers are inside the binary: there is nothing more to install) and writes the files, the imports between them, the packages they use, and what it could not read. It is a fact sheet for an agent (or you) drafting a LikeC4 model of a codebase that has none; it never writes the model itself. See [scan format](docs/scan.md).

A second skill, the behavior skill (`/pathlight:behavior`), teaches an agent to draw what a user sees as a state diagram (a `*.behavior.c4` file that `draft` leaves alone), mark states it found broken (`#bug`, red) or repaired (`#fixed`, green), and record the commit it read the code at. It is the agent's reading of the code, not a scan, and says so. The map skill (`plugins/claude/skills/map/SKILL.md`, `/pathlight:map`) teaches an agent this workflow: scan, draft the model and mapping, check until clean, show. The Claude plugin ships all three (
