## Observe live activity

Place `.pathlight/pathlight.activity.json` in the agent's workspace. This repository includes a mapping to its own `pathlight` LikeC4 project (`examples/viewer`).
Mappings use workspace-relative path globs and exact LikeC4 element IDs:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "project": "my-project",
  "mappings": [{ "glob": "services/payments/**", "element": "platform.payments" }],
  "ignore": ["tests/**", "vendor/**"],
  "shared": ["platform.types"]
}
```

`ignore` lists files deliberately outside the model (the viewer leaves their activity out too), and `shared` lists elements anything may import (so `pathlight check` expects no relationship to them). `planned` lists elements designed but not built yet (their mappings may match no files without being a mistake; `check` reports how much of the plan exists and the viewer draws them dashed with a `[planned]` tag until they have files). `entries` lists views meant to be opened directly (not linked from another), which `check` does not count as a second entry point. `resources` lists the elements that are what the code talks to, each with the packages that lead to it (`{ "element": "postgresql", "packages": ["pg"] }`); `check` judges a relationship to one by those imports. `check` reads these; the viewer also reads `ignore` and `planned`.

In OpenCode with `record: true`, just run `/pathlight-open live`. Without it, ask the agent to show the `pathlight` project's `live` view with `live: true` and your current pane ID.
The plugin binds the panel to the session. It records that session's subsequent tool starts, completions, and failures automatically.
Call `pathlight_stop` to stop recording. Closing the viewer alone does not stop recording.
Plugin reloads stop recording; call `show` with `live: true` again to resume.
Subagent sessions are separate and are not automatically included.

The Work card lists the selected component's recent mapped edits and commands (three rows; repeats collapse to `×N`), and the session summary (`c`) lists edits to files no component claims under `not in the model` (files in the mapping's `ignore` list are skipped). Reads, and calls that name no file (a subagent launch, a search), are recorded but not shown live.
Native cards also carry a tag in their top border while a tool runs (`■ edit`, `▸` command), then `✓ done` or `✗ failed` for 30 seconds. Groups display their own mapped activity in their title.
The layout stays fixed as activity arrives.
In the header line a call on a file no component claims shows without a component. Long-running calls become `unconfirmed` after 30 seconds without an outcome.
This is an observation-age indicator, not proof that the agent disconnected or the tool stopped.
Selection, pan and zoom remain unchanged as activity arrives. Reopening the viewer reads retained activity.

For Claude Code, `pathlight init` installs these hooks. To do it by hand, copy the hooks from `plugins/claude/hooks.example.json` into your project settings and replace the absolute plugin path.
Merge the hooks with existing settings; do not replace unrelated configuration.
The hook runs asynchronously and exits successfully even if observation fails.
`pathlight plan <element ids>` lets an agent say where it is about to work; the viewer outlines those elements and marks activity outside them `off plan`. A `Stop` hook runs `pathlight refresh` after each turn: one scan for the check (the viewer's out-of-date badge), then, on a map `pathlight draft` drew, a redraw when files landed where no box claims them, a planned box got its files, or a box's files are gone, and the diff (connectors whose imports changed since the last commit; `pathlight diff [--base REV]` prints the same list) (see [native viewer](docs/native-viewer.md)). A redraw keeps every name, writes nothing when nothing changed, never touches a model a person wrote, and is held back when it would remove a box a journey uses (`pathlight check` says which). `pathlight config set redraw off --workspace .` turns it off for one workspace. On a drawn map `pathlight plan --new FOLDER --title TEXT` declares a part before it exists: a dashed box with that name until its files land; `pathlight plan --drop FOLDER` takes back one nobody built. When a redraw draws boxes nobody has named, the hook (Claude Code's `asyncRewake`; OpenCode's plugin sends its own message) asks the agent once to hand them to the namer, at most six a turn. The adapter accepts `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, and `PostToolUseFailure`; the tests use hook payloads, and it records real interactive Claude Code sessions on Linux.
With the Claude session ID, open a bound viewer:

```sh
bun run pathlight show VIEW --workspace /path/to/project --project PROJECT --pane %ID --source claude --session SESSION_ID
```

Only tool names, call/session IDs, workspace-relative paths, operation categories, timestamps, and lifecycle states are retained.
Tool arguments, command strings, source contents, tool results, and error text are not stored.
Records live under `.cache/pathlight/activity` in directories created with private permissions.

The OpenCode observer uses a bounded 128-event queue and supports eight opted-in sessions per plugin instance.
Collection is best-effort: overload or disk failures may lose events, and old history is pruned. It is not an audit log.
All activity remains local. No background service or network endpoint is installed.

[Pathlight](https://github.com/dumbbunnyio/pathlight) for OpenCode: an architecture diagram beside your conversation that lights up the components the agent reads and edits, and a Sonnet-sized tracer agent that records how something works as a flow.

This package is the OpenCode side only. It needs the `pathlight` binary on your PATH:

```sh
npm i -g pathlight
```

(or, without Node, `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dumbbunnyio/pathlight/main/install.sh | sh`).

Then let `pathlight` add this plugin to your global OpenCode config for every project:

pathlight init --global

Or add it to one project's `opencode.json` yourself (`record: true` turns on observation of that workspace's sessions; leave it out to record only when asked):

{ "plugins": [{ "package": "@dumbbunnyio/pathlight-opencode", "options": { "record": true } }] }

It is pinned to the newest Sonnet-class model you can use. If you have none, it runs on your current model; ask the agent to run `pathlight_models`, or set it yourself:

```json
{ "plugins": [{ "package": "@dumbbunnyio/pathlight-opencode", "options": { "tracerModel": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5" } }] }
```

Only Sonnet-class models have been measured doing this well (Sonnet passed 4 of 5 test traces, Haiku 1 of 5; see the Pathlight repository, `docs/eval.md`).

# Measuring map quality

Pathlight is only as useful as its map is true, so the map is measured, not judged. Nothing here asks a model for an opinion: each number is counted from the scan, from `pathlight check`, from the computed LikeC4 views, or from rules a repository's own authors wrote down. The tools live in `tests/eval/` (development tools, not shipped).

## A pinned repository

```sh
git clone --local --no-hardlinks <path-to-opencode> .cache/eval/opencode-installed   # .cache is git-ignored
git -C .cache/eval/opencode-installed checkout 5fa426f68d                            # always the same commit
(cd .cache/eval/opencode-installed && bun install --ignore-scripts --frozen-lockfile)   # lets the reference resolver follow workspace packages
```

## Do the facts match an independent answer?

```sh
bun tests/eval/facts.ts --workspace .cache/eval/opencode-installed --out /tmp/facts-diff.json
```

Compares `pathlight scan` with a reference made another way: every import found by a pattern match and resolved by `oxc-resolver` (a different resolver, with each package's own tsconfig). Both disagreement lists are printed for reading in the source; neither side is assumed right. On the pinned `opencode` (5,127 files, about 19,400 connections) every disagreement was explained: the reference counts import statements that sit inside string literals (test fixtures, code generators) and cannot follow `?raw` or runtime-conditional `exports`; the scan had one real bug (an import with more than 400 tokens of names was dropped), now fixed and tested.

## Does a model agree with the code and with what the authors say?

```sh
bun src/cli.ts draft --workspace .cache/eval/opencode-installed
bun tests/eval/run.ts --workspace .cache/eval/opencode-installed --reference tests/eval/references/opencode.json
```

Reports, for any workspace's model and mapping: files claimed, relationships an import supports, element pairs the imports connect that no relationship declares, how many dependency rules the authors state still hold (`tests/eval/references/opencode.json`: each rule quotes the document line it comes from), and how many boxes the busiest views hold. For a draft made from imports the first three are true by construction; they matter for agent-written and hand-written models. The rules and the view sizes are the informative numbers for a draft.

**Re-exports followed (2026-10-26).** The scan now follows each imported name through a package's barrel files to the file that declares it (see [scan format](scan.md#what-it-follows)), found when a live first run on opentui drew every binding pointing only at `core`'s `index.ts`. ## Flows: does an agent's journey match the code?

A journey (`pathlight flow add`) is an agent's reading of the code, so it is scored the same way as the map: counted, not judged. `pathlight flows` already finds what can be shown wrong or old (a file that is gone or changed since the sync commit, a hop with no model relationship). It cannot tell that a well-formed journey is wrong, so the eval adds the questions it cannot answer.

```sh
bun tests/eval/flows.ts --workspace DIR --reference tests/eval/references/flows.json
```

`tests/eval/references/flows.json` holds a few questions about this repository ("what happens when someone runs `pathlight check`?"), each with the hops of a correct trace and the files a trace has to read. The answer is the scorer's own hand reading of the code, not an agent's. For each journey the scorer reports:

- **Hops matched, missed, and in order** against the answer.
- **Invented**: a hop outside the answer *and* with nothing behind it (no model relationship, or no import joining the two components through a file the agent says it read). The pass mark is zero.
- **Additional**: a hop outside the answer that the model and an import both back. It is a different reading to look at, and does not count against the run.
- **Unbacked / unsupported**: hops without a model relationship; hops without an import in either direction (data can flow against the import, as in the viewer reading the journal).
- **Files**: cited files that do not exist, and whether the key files were read.

A run passes when every hop of the answer is present and in order, nothing is invented, every hop is backed and supported, no cited file is missing and every key file was read. A hop the answer marks `over` (http, websocket, process) is exempt from backed and supported, because the import-drawn map cannot hold it. It is still required and reported on its own line (since 2026-10-28). `tests/eval-flows.test.ts` plants one defect at a time (no journey, a missing hop, hops in the wrong order, an invented hop, a hop with a relationship but no import, a missing file, an unread key file) and requires the scorer to notice each.

What each check can and cannot see:

| Defect | `pathlight flows` | this score |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A cited file is gone or changed since the sync commit | yes | yes (gone) |
| A hop with no model relationship | yes (`≠`) | yes |
| No sync note | yes | no |
| A hop between related components that the code does not make | no | yes, if no import joins them through a cited file |
| Hops in the wrong order | no | yes |
| A real hop left out | no | yes |

Neither can tell that an event title is right, or that a hop is the *only* way the code gets from A to B.

# Use the native diagram viewer

This is the reference for every key and screen. To start, read the one-screen [quick start](quick-start.md).

The native renderer is the default for `pathlight show` and `pathlight view`. It is the only renderer and draws interactive nodes without images.

From the repository root, run this command in a terminal:

```sh
bun run pathlight view live --project pathlight
```

Click a node. Its border becomes white, and the details panel lists its incoming and outgoing relationships.
Connections are made of horizontal and vertical lines with rounded bends. Quiet ones are dotted, and the selected node's are solid: cyan for incoming, amber for outgoing.
The details use the same colors, node names, and full relationship labels. Scroll over the details to read wrapped labels without panning the diagram.
Click a node or use `h`, `j`, `k` and `l`, which select the nearest node left, down, up or right of the selection (siblings are preferred; ancestors and descendants are reached with Backspace and Enter). The camera only moves if the new node would be off screen. Arrow keys pan the camera without changing the selection, and Shift+`hjkl` pans too. Press `v` to swap the roles: arrows select, `hjkl` pan.
Enter goes into a box: into its children when this view draws them (a group, or the frame the view is about), else into the view it opens; `o` opens that view even when the children are drawn here, and the inspector says `o opens VIEW` only then. After Enter into a group, `b` or backspace reselects the group before anything else. When the view a box opens leaves smaller boxes out, the inspector says so under the counts (`4 smaller boxes are not drawn in its view`).
Press `b` or Backspace to return to the previous view, selection, zoom, and scroll position: the two keys are one stack. With nowhere to go back to, Backspace goes up instead: to the group that holds the selection in this view, else to the view whose box opens this one (that box selected); `b` says `No previous view`.
Press `f` to fit the diagram, `r` to center the selection, and `q` to quit.
Press `+` or `=` to zoom in, `-` to zoom out, and `0` to return to 100%.
Zoom keeps the viewport center in place. Keyboard pan, reveal, and zoom ease into position using a Three orthographic camera.
Hierarchy and search navigation reveal a group's upper-left corner or center a leaf.
Press `i` to toggle the inspector. From 120 columns up it is docked beside the diagram (drag its divider to resize it) and open by default. Under 120 columns with 40 rows or more (the pane beside Claude Code's transcript, a tall tmux split) it is docked below the diagram instead, a little under half the rows, the same head, cards and question line, and open by default; the diagram keeps the full width. Narrower, shorter terminals start without it; `i` (or a section number) shows it as an overlay on the right half, covering part of the diagram, and `i` or Esc hides it again. PageUp/PageDown scroll its contents. Press `?` for keyboard help: first what each connector color means, drawn in those colors, three to a row in the tiers' columns with a rule under them, then every key, in three tiers named for how far along you are with this codebase. **Understand it** (select with a click or a neighbor, `tab` through the inspector or a flow's steps, enter into a box, `o` the view a box opens, `b` and backspace back where you were or else up, `t` ask how it works or tell it what to change (one key, listed once), `F` step through a flow (from the talk, it turns the column to the node face; `i` goes back), `?`); **Direct it** (`c` what it did this session, and the review, `a` follow, `w` jump to the work, `e` files, `/` search (views, boxes, journeys, files; `tab` picks the kind), `g` views, `i` inspector or talk, `z` widen the talk, `f` `0` `+ -` `r` and the pan keys); **Shape the map** (`d` trace a flow, `m` improve the map, `n` name it yourself, `p` replay, `s` subagent calls, `T` themes, `1`–`4` and the keys inside a card, `v`, `q`). From 100 columns the tiers stand side by side, below that they stack. The tier you have reached (the highest one you have pressed a key of in this session) is in the accent color. The footer and empty states only ever name keys from the first tier.

The diagram is fitted and centered when it opens and whenever the terminal is resized, until you pan, zoom (`+`, `-`, `0`) or recenter (`r`) yourself; `f` fits it again and turns that back on. Switching views fits the new view. Fit zooms a small view in to fill the screen, but never above 150% (text does not grow with the cards), and it takes the connectors in as well as the cards.

A view is drawn with **compact fit** (`src/viewer/compact.ts`): LikeC4's arrangement (the order of cards on both axes, which cards share a rank, nesting, which side an edge leaves) with Pathlight's spacing and card sizes. Every card in a view is one size: the widest title decides it (on one or two lines, one when that costs at most two columns more; at least its longest word plus padding, from 20 to 32 columns), and the most lines any title takes at that width decide the height, so a short title has a blank row beneath it. The space between cards shrinks to 6 columns and 2 rows, more where group frames stand between them; a group is the box around its children with its frame and a clear cell. A view that still does not fit at 100% is fitted below it, with every card still one size: a card's cells come from its corner and its size, so zoom never changes one card's rows or columns without changing them all. A card's first row says what matters about it: a box that opens a view says how many boxes are inside it, the count in brackets (`[36]`, a package on the overview too), a resource (a database, queue or third-party API the draft drew from the code's imports) says what kind of thing it is (`database`, `cache`, `queue`, `storage`, `search`, `mail`, `identity`, `monitoring`, `ai`, `service`), any other leaf says nothing, and no other card names its kind; while a session is watched, the same row holds the read and edit counts. The row is in every card of a view or none (a view whose cards differ in kind keeps it, blank on a leaf, so its layout does not change). The observed tag stays in the top border. When the zoom gives cards fewer rows than the layout did, that row goes from every card (before a line of a title), and a title that no longer fits ends in `…`.

A view opens on its entry: the subject of a neighborhood view, else the node the most connectors leave, else the first node that links to another view, else the first node.

Under 80 columns a diagram does not fit, so the nodes are listed instead: one row per node, indented by depth, with its kind (or its `[edit]`/`[read]`/`[run]` state while a tool runs) at the right. ↑↓ (or j k) move the selection down the list, Enter and Backspace go into a group and up to its parent, and clicking a row selects it. Search, ask, help and the inspector overlay work as usual.

Click an inspector section header once to focus it and again to fold it. Headers read `▾ 1 Connects ──── 4`: the number is the key that focuses the card (dim while it is folded, amber while it has focus).

Colors are 24-bit. When `COLORTERM` does not say `truecolor` or `24bit` (and `TERM` is not a direct-color type), every color is snapped to the nearest xterm-256 color; set `PATHLIGHT_COLORS=256` or `PATHLIGHT_COLORS=truecolor` to force either.

## Themes

Press `T` to choose a theme. The list previews each one live over the diagram as you move (up/down, PageUp/PageDown, Home/End); Enter keeps it and remembers it, Esc puts the previous one back. The choice is saved as `"theme": "name"` in `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pathlight/config.json` (default `~/.config/pathlight/config.json`), beside the Claude plugin's `"claude"` choice; nothing about any workspace is stored there. `PATHLIGHT_THEME=name` overrides it for one run.

Themes use [OpenCode's theme format](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode), so its themes work unchanged: a JSON file with `defs` (named colors) and `theme` (roles mapped to a hex color, a `defs` name, another role, an ANSI color number, `transparent`, or `{ "dark": …, "light": … }`). Only the roles Pathlight draws with are read (`background`, `backgroundPanel`, `backgroundElement`, `text`, `textMuted`, `border`, `borderActive`, `borderSubtle`, `primary`, `accent`, `secondary`, `info`, `warning`, `success`, `error`); the diff, markdown and syntax roles are ignored. Pathlight's own shades (`grid`, `hot`, `pick`, `edgeDim`, `cardEdge`, `keycap`, `scrim`) are blended from those unless a theme sets them. `incoming` (live, search) is nudged away from `accent` (selection) when a theme gives them nearly the same color. A color with an alpha channel (`#rrggbbaa`) is laid over the theme's background.

- Built in: `pathlight` (the original look, the default) and the 32 themes bundled in `src/themes/` (copied from OpenCode, MIT, see `NOTICE.md`).
- Your own: put `name.json` in `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pathlight/themes/` or `<workspace>/.pathlight/themes/`. A workspace theme beats a user theme beats a bundled one of the same name. A file that does not parse is skipped; a theme that cannot be resolved (an unknown reference, a cycle) is refused with a message naming it.
- `system` takes the terminal's own background, foreground and ANSI colors. They are requested once at startup (OSC 4/10/11); the entry appears in the picker only if the terminal answers, and inside tmux that needs `set -g allow-passthrough on`. Verified only against fixed color values so far, not against a range of terminals.
- Light or dark: themes with both variants follow the terminal's background when it reports one; `PATHLIGHT_MODE=dark|light` forces it. Many themes define only one variant.
- With `COLORTERM` unset, colors are still snapped to xterm-256 for whichever theme is active.
Resize the terminal, then click another visible node to check that mouse targets stay aligned.

Press `/` to search everything: every view, every box (in any view, nested or not), every journey and every file the mapping gives a box, with the views and files outside the one you are in included. `tab` narrows the list to one kind and on round (all → views → boxes → journeys → files → all; `shift-tab` goes back): the picker's title names the chosen kind in the accent with the others dimmed beside it, so you see what the next `tab` gives. Choosing a journey reads it as `F` would, in the view that draws its steps apart. `F` still steps to the next journey. `g` opens the same list restricted to views.
Type to narrow it. Matching ignores case. Several words must all match, the letters of a word may be spread out (`ctx` finds `context`), and a swapped or doubled letter (`hepler`) still finds `helper`. A box matches on its name and its id, a view on its own name (the part of its title after the last ` / `, as the draft titles a view of something inside another `Holder / Own name`) and, a little weaker, on its whole title and its id, and a file on its name and its path. A view's row reads its own name first and the holder after it, dimmed and cut first, as a file's row reads its name and then its folder; its node count stays at the right. The picker's frame is at most 100 columns wide, and its right-hand column is as wide as its longest row needs, up to 26.
Results are ranked by how well the text matches and by where the result is, added together. Match quality counts most: an exact name or id comes first wherever it is, then a prefix or a word start, then a substring, then spread-out letters. Where it is breaks ties and nudges close calls, in this order: a box in the view you are in, a file in it, a box elsewhere, a journey, a view, a file elsewhere. A row for something in your view carries a dot (`● here`); a row elsewhere says which view it opens. Files the mapping ignores (tests, generated code) are not offered. The ranking constants and their tests are in `src/search.ts` and `tests/search.test.ts`.
Up, Down, `Ctrl+N`/`Ctrl+P`, PgUp, PgDn, Home and End move; Enter goes; Escape (or a click outside) closes without changing anything. A box in the view you are in is selected where it is. Otherwise Enter opens the view of its parent, else its own view, else a view it is linked from, else the smallest view that has it, selects the box, and Back returns. A file opens its box with that file marked in the Files section. A view just opens.
The list scrolls inside its frame (the border shows `79–95 of 95`). Typing, pasted text (256 characters at most) and resizing all work while it is open, `q`, `b` and `o` are text rather than commands, and diagram clicks do not change the selection. Ctrl+C still quits.

## Plan

`pathlight plan ELEMENT ...` records the elements an agent is about to work on in `.cache/pathlight/plan.json` (ids only, at most 64, each checked against the model; no ids clears it). The viewer outlines those nodes (and their containers) in purple, adds `plan N` to the breadcrumb, and tags any node with observed activity that is outside the plan `off plan`. It is intent, not observation: it never changes what the activity shows. A plan set more than two hours before the watched session began (or, with no session, more than two hours ago) is not shown, so one left over from earlier work never tags today's.

`pathlight point ELEMENT [--view VIEW] [--journey ID --step N]` is how an agent walking a person through the map (the onboarding skill, `/pathlight:onboarding`) shows them a box: it writes the element (an id from the model, or a box's key from `pathlight brief`), the view if one was named, the journey and step if given (checked against `pathlight flows`), and the time to `.cache/pathlight/point.json`, and nothing else. The viewer reads it twice a second and acts on each pointer once: it selects the element in the view named, else in this view, else in the view that draws it (with a Back entry; no notice, the header's title says where), reveals it, and the header says `← agent: <title>` beside the view's name until the next key. It never changes the column's face (a talk showing stays showing), it is let go while a modal is open or the talk's field has the keys, and nothing afterwards follows the agent: a later pointer is a new, single request. A pointer with a journey and a step turns flow mode on at that step, as `F` would (in the view that draws the journey's steps apart, the step reader open, the `← agent` mark as before), and the viewer stays in it until `esc` or the next pointer; a pointer without a journey leaves a journey the last pointer turned on. A journey written a moment ago is read before the pointer is acted on. A pointer older than the viewer is ignored; `pathlight point` with no element clears the mark. With no viewer open on the workspace the command writes nothing and says so. The skill asks before its first point.

## Review: new dependencies

After each turn the Stop hook's `pathlight refresh` runs the diff, which lists imports between two components that the model has no relationship for and that the last commit did not have. While any wait for a verdict the header says `▲ N new dependencies · c review` (with an out-of-date check, one badge: `▲ 2 new dependencies · 3 files not in the model · c review`, shortened to `▲ 2 new dependencies · out of date · c review`, then the count alone), and `c` opens the review above the session summary: one row per dependency with an import that makes it. `j`/`k` move, `e` opens that import in the editor at its line, `y` accepts and `n` rejects.

- Rejecting types a request into the agent's pane (the one `pathlight show` was given) to take the dependency out, or to say what bigger change that needs and wait. The row stays, marked `rejected · still in the code`, until a later diff no longer finds it.
- Accepting on a map someone wrote asks the agent to add the relationship to the model. On a drafted map (whose arrows are the imports) nothing is sent: once every new dependency is accepted, and none rejected is still in the code, the map is redrawn from the code, so a redraw never draws one you have not seen.
- Verdicts are kept in `.cache/pathlight/decisions.json`, so a pair is never asked about twice. They record what the person decided, not whether the code is right; the evidence is static imports only.


## Rendering limits

Pass a view ID and use `--workspace` and `--project` to select its model.
Empty views are rejected. Native mode does not support collapsing groups, relationship-link navigation, or editing the model.
The framebuffer follows the terminal viewport rather than allocating a full-diagram canvas. Manual zoom ranges from 12.5% to 800%; fit never goes above 150% and can go below 12.5% to show the whole diagram.
Leaf shapes become filled boxes. Groups become transparent outlines with titles, ordered behind their children.
Labels wrap at cell boundaries and can be clipped on small nodes. Leaf labels hide below six columns or two rows.
Connectors are routed orthogonally around leaf nodes and rasterized onto terminal cells each frame; where no clear route exists they fall back to a plain horizontal-vertical-horizontal path. Unselected connections remain dim; selected ones draw last. Arrowheads occupy the cell next to the target node; dot and diamond markers are drawn as plain arrowheads.
Relationship labels wrap in the scrollable selection panel rather than covering the diagram.
At 100%, coordinates use 16 horizontal pixels per terminal cell. Vertical scale follows the reported terminal cell aspect ratio, falling back to 32 pixels. Nodes and connectors share the camera projection.
Resizing changes the viewport, not the graph layout. Native boxes and scrolling still move at terminal-cell boundaries during easing.
The activity journal is best-effort. Calls without outcomes stop showing as active after 30 seconds, and the activity panel marks them unconfirmed.

## Implementation and verification

Native node boxes, group outlines, and a connector framebuffer share a clipped viewport. Hit testing uses displayed cell bounds, including rounded group titles.
Camera interpolation uses OpenTUI frame callbacks and Three's orthographic camera for the projection. Nothing is drawn by Three or the GPU, so no WebGPU backend is needed. Linux is the verified platform.
LikeC4 parent and child IDs drive hierarchy navigation. Renderable boxes remain siblings with absolute coordinates to avoid nested border offsets.
The isolated tmux tests exercise the flat view and both nested Parcel views, including clicks before and after pan and resize, independent group and child activity, and normal process exit.
The file-browser test requires `nvim` and checks an actual save, resizing during editing, editor failure recovery, file filtering, refresh, and preserved zoomed diagram position.
The Linux editor lifecycle test checks launcher environment forwarding and shutdown of an editor wrapper with a child process.
Navigation tests verify explicit links, rejected empty destinations, restoration of zoomed diagram cells and selection, an unchanged process, and activity updates after returning.
Search tests exercise the ranking (an exact match beats the current view, the current view beats the rest on equal matches, typos, several words), shortcut isolation, pasted text, mouse isolation, resize, going to a view, and closing back to the original diagram cells.
Routing tests check that routes are only horizontal and vertical, avoid nodes in the way, merge into junctions and end in an arrowhead outside the target. The relationship test checks selection colors and long labels that scroll without moving the diagram.
The interactive prototype was manually tried and approved before integration into the CLI. macOS and broader terminal compatibility remain unverified.

## Design principle (user decision, 2026-10-21)

The viewer must be informative, not a data dump: an engineer following a harness's work should see an elegant, intuitive picture with the detail available on request. The inspector was redesigned on 2026-10-24 (Phase 1): it ranks what it shows (the component, what it is doing now, what it connects to) and keeps files, history and the session summary one key away, and live work appears as a tag in each card's border and a `now`/`last` line in the header. Phase 2 (flow mode: a flow drawn on the diagram with a step reader, cards off the path dimmed, `≠` where a journey hop has no relationship in the model) was added the same day; flows are readings of the code, labeled so and kept apart from what the journal observed. The out-of-date badge, diff marks, plan outline and `off plan` tags added on 2026-10-21 are provisional and may still move or merge.

Since the design pass (2026-11-02) the screen says each thing in one place and in one vocabulary. **Header line 1** is where you are: the view's title, and in journey mode `◇ <journey> · 2/5 · <the step's box>`, with `← agent` when the agent pointed there; at its right only what warns or asks for a decision (`▲ out of date`, `▲ N new dependencies · c review`), then `✓ in sync` and `● live`, without detail. **Header line 2** is `N boxes · back N` and, at its right, the news line: what the agent and the session are doing now (the call running, `following <box>  a stop`, or the `w` offer). **The footer** is the mode, the selection and the reply to a key the person pressed, or the keys of the mode; nothing the agent did is reported there. On screen a flow is a journey, a node is a box, and the spelling is American. Work is edits and commands: reads stay in the journal, `c` and replay, and show nowhere live. The inspector's head is the name, the words, at most one caveat from the scan and the `o` action; no kind word and no counts. A suggested question is ghost text in an empty field that `→` takes.

## Involvement, not spectating (user decision, 2026-10-26)

With agents writing most of the code, a developer risks only watching text and diffs roll by. Pathlight's two use cases are understanding a repository you have never seen, visually, and making changes to it while seeing what is touched. It involves the person at the moments that need their judgement, and is quiet otherwise: the end-of-turn review asks them to accept or reject each new dependency the code gained (static imports, never a claim about behavior), and reading the code behind a decision is one key away in their own editor (`e` on a flow step, on a dependency under review, or a changed file). Accuracy comes first, and options are added only when a decision cannot be made without them.

## What we are trying to achieve

Give a developer working with an AI coding agent a persistent, navigable view of
the system beside the conversation. The developer should be able to answer:

- Where does this component sit in the architecture?
- What does it depend on, and what depends on it?
- Which explicitly mapped files implement it?
- Where is the bound agent session reading or editing right now, according to
  the tool events we actually received?

The diagram should be a working interface, not a picture the agent generates and
forgets. Moving between architecture, source files and the conversation should
not require losing orientation or reopening the viewer.

## The intended working loop

1. Open a LikeC4 view beside the coding conversation in an owned tmux pane.
2. Explore with selection, search, pan/zoom, group/parent navigation and explicit
   linked views. Inspect incoming/outgoing relationships without obscuring nodes.
3. Select a component, browse its mapped files, filter the list, and open a file
   in the developer's editor. Return to the same diagram context afterward.
4. Optionally bind the viewer to an opted-in agent session. See mapped READ/EDIT
   activity and observed outcomes without changing layout, selection or camera.
5. Follow a linked detail view and return with Back, restoring the previous
   selection and camera. Reuse the owned pane for a new requested view safely.

The keys come in three tiers, named for how far along the developer is with this codebase, and `?` shows them in that order (implemented 2026-10-28): **understand it** (select, move, ask how something works with `t`, step through a flow with `F`), **direct it** (`t` again to tell the agent what to change, follow, review, files, search, views), **shape the map** (trace, improve or name a box, replay, themes). The footer and empty states name only the first tier. `t` closes its loop either way: a question whose answer is a path is answered in chat and recorded as a journey drawn on the map, and an instruction is declared (`pathlight plan`, a planned element for anything new) before the first edit. Both are rules in the request the viewer types and in the map skill; whether an agent follows them is measured by the flows eval and live runs, not assumed.

This loop is supported today through the CLI, with OpenCode integration and a
Claude hook adapter. The Claude adapter has payload-based tests and records
real interactive Claude Code sessions on Linux (its plugin hooks wrote this
repository's own journals).

## Accepted design

### Architecture comes from LikeC4

LikeC4 owns element IDs, relationships, hierarchy and the diagram's arrangement
(order, ranks, nesting, which side an edge leaves); the spacing and card sizes
are Pathlight's (compact fit). Navigation
between views follows explicit links. File attribution comes from explicit
workspace mappings, not agent guesses or title matching.

What the code talks to that is not code (databases, caches, queues, object
stores, search, mail, identity providers, monitoring, AI providers, named
third-party APIs) is drawn from evidence only: a resource exists where a file
imports a package that one table of data (`src/resources/imports.json`) leads
to it, with an arrow from each component that does (implemented 2026-11-09,
plan `phase-r-resources`, step 1). Type-only imports and tests are no
evidence; HTTP clients lead nowhere. A resource's mapped files are its schema
(`*.sql`, `*.prisma`), never the code that calls it, so an edit lights the
code it was made in. The map says what the code expects, never what anyone
has access to. Compose files and the example environment are read as names
only (images, environment names; never a value): they confirm what the code
reaches, name an ORM's database when they name one engine, and add a box only
for a datastore they run with no code found, which it says (step 2,
2026-11-09). Helm charts (dependencies, values' images, secrets named by their kind) and Terraform (resource and module block headers by type) were added in step 3 the same day; prose (a README saying what a secret is for) is not read. A repository with no code the scan reads (only charts or compose files) is drafted as one view of the resources they declare rather than refused, and what only infrastructure declares is on the overview of any drafted repository. Phase R2 (2026-11-09): in a repository that is mostly infrastructure (more programs than code files), the Helm workloads and compose services it runs are drawn as `container` boxes inside their chart or compose file, with arrows to the resources their files name, judged by `check` against those files; arrows between programs are not drawn (a start order is not a call). Phase R3 (2026-11-10): each resource with a user opens a view of who uses it (`<resource>_users`, enter on its card), drawn from the same arrows, with only the arrows into it; a view, not a new mode, so both viewers, Back and `pathlight show` have it unchanged.

### The primary experience is genuinely interactive terminal UI

OpenTUI renders nodes, groups, labels and an inspector. Three supplies the eased
orthographic camera; orthogonal thin-line connectors with rounded bends
connect the nodes. They share the same projection so picking and connectors remain
aligned as the developer moves around.

The user approved the Three camera, the orthogonal thin-line appearance, polished inspector and
restored workflows. Preserve these together. A prior ScrollBox-based camera was
rejected because its movement did not match the approved experiment. Replacing
the camera again requires a demonstrated improvement and explicit approval,
not merely an equivalent feature checklist.

The inspector adapts between side and bottom layouts, supports a draggable
divider, and can be hidden. Linux usability and visual quality take priority;
narrow terminals must remain usable rather than being treated as an afterthought.

### Live activity means observed agent work—not runtime telemetry

Events describe tool starts and outcomes mapped to architecture elements. A read
or edit may pulse the affected node; it does not demonstrate traffic along a
relationship. A successful tool call is not proof of passing tests or correctness.

Activity is best-effort, bounded and local. Unmapped work remains unmapped.
Old unfinished calls become unconfirmed rather than being presented as proof
that a tool is still running. A group shows its own mapped activity, not an
automatic roll-up of its children.

Workspace, project, source and session attribution must prevent unrelated work
from appearing in the viewer. Viewing is distinct from recording: opening a
bound CLI viewer consumes retained events, and closing it does not stop an
already-enabled observer. No source code or tool payloads belong in the journal.

### Talking to the agent beside the diagram (implemented 2026-10-29)

Beside the conversation (a tmux split beside the agent's pane, Claude Code's pane at every width) `t`, `m` and `d` ask in a modal, since the reply lands in the conversation already on screen (design pass, 2026-11-02, decided by David: "modal when not full screen because the user can already see a window with claude/opencode, when full screen, we can show it to them"). Where the conversation is hidden, the viewer's tmux window zoomed, the inspector's column has a second face, the talk: `t`, `m` and `d` open it, and it shows the bound session's conversation (the person's prompts and the agent's text, in order, with their times) above a field. The first request of a talk is the same line `t`, `m` or `d` always typed into the agent's pane; later ones are the typed text alone. The reply is read from the host's own conversation file (Claude Code's transcript, OpenCode's database) while the talk is open in this run, held in memory and never copied; the hooks record only where that file is, whether the agent is waiting for the person in its pane, and when its turn ended. A state line says `working`, `waiting for you in its pane` or `done`. What it does not do: it calls no model and stores no prose; it shows no tool calls, results, thinking or subagent turns; permission prompts and the host's own dialogs are answered in the agent's pane, not in the talk; it never moves the camera, the selection or the column on a reply. Full screen is tmux's pane zoom, or, in Claude Code, the pane beside the transcript (below).

### Pathlight inside Claude Code (implemented 2026-10-31; experimental and off by default since 2026-11-01)

By default `/pathlight:open` opens the tmux viewer beside the conversation, as it always did. `/pathlight:open pane`, or `pathlight config set claude pane` for good, draws the viewer in Claude Code's own pane instead, docked beside the transcript in the fullscreen layout from 110 columns and inline above the prompt on the main screen, bound to that conversation (`$.session.id()`, never `--follow`). Shelved as experimental by David on 2026-11-01: Claude Code caps a docked pane at 45% of the terminal and its mods API offers no way to resize or place it, which is not an effective viewport for the diagram; the work, its tests and its goldens are kept for when that changes, and nothing of it runs unless chosen. The viewer is `pathlight pane`: the same viewer on a headless renderer, its frames sent to the plugin, the person's keys sent back; the talk's request is submitted as the person's own prompt with the text `show` types, and the reply is read from the transcript as before. With the pane chosen, the agent's own `pathlight show`/`open` opens the same pane; `/pathlight:open tmux` or a terminal too small for the pane opens the tmux pane. Under 120 columns the talk is a modal there (the reply is in the transcript beside it). What it does not do: the pane takes no clicks on the diagram, Escape is Claude Code's (`q` leaves a mode there), it opens no editor (files open from the tmux viewer), the docked pane is at most 45% of the terminal's width (the inspector below the diagram under 120 columns), and it records, follows and calls nothing. Desired, not built: an OpenCode equivalent (OpenCode has no pane API; the tmux pane remains there).

### The map in a browser (step 1 implemented 2026-11-08, the launch 2026-11-08)

`pathlight web` serves the terminal viewer to a browser on `127.0.0.1`: the same layout, words, colors and keys, decided on the server by the terminal's own functions and drawn by a small page (Solid) that owns only the pixels and the camera. `B`, `pathlight web --open` and `/pathlight:open web` open it in one app window per workspace, in Pathlight's own browser profile; its server stops when that window closes. It exists so the same page can later sit inside an editor (a VS Code webview) beside the code. Implemented: the map, the inspector, the views, Back, the keys for those, the themes, and the agent's live work (card tags and the pulse of a running call, the news line, Work, follow and `w`, with the same rules as the terminal: reads shown nowhere live, nothing moves unless follow is on), and live reload keeping each window's camera and selection. Desired, not built: journeys, the review and the talk in the browser, then the VS Code extension. Not a hosted service: local, one workspace, no accounts.

### The first day (implemented 2026-10-29)

The first run ends with a briefing for a person new to the code: `pathlight brief --first-day` prints what the app is, how it is built, where the project declares it starts, the journeys to follow and how sure the names are, derived each time from the scan, the agent's names and notes and the recorded journeys. Nothing new is stored, and it says so when a part is empty. The onboarding skill (`/pathlight:onboarding`) then walks the person through the map: the briefing as printed, then the recorded journeys step by step, ending with one line naming the boxes no journey touched, facts first, one file read narrowly when needed, boxes cited by key and files by line, what was read kept apart from what was inferred. With the person's agreement it moves the diagram with `pathlight point`, which selects one box once and marks it `← agent` until their next key; it never makes the viewer follow the agent. What it is not: no graph of symbols or routes, no model called by Pathlight (the agent reads, the viewer only points), no git ownership, and it edits nothing (names come only through the namer, journeys only through the tracer). Whether the journey-first order works for newcomers is still to be measured on real walks.

### Continuity and safe ownership are product features

Search cancellation, linked-view history and editor return preserve orientation.
Activity must not recenter the camera. External editors own input while active.
Shutdown must clean up owned resources and editor process groups, without
touching the user's conversation or a pane repurposed for another command.

## What “working” means

Changes must preserve these observable outcomes:

| Outcome | Evidence to seek |
| --- | --- |
| Developer can explore without losing orientation | Search cancel and Back restore selection, pan and zoom; resize keeps interaction aligned |
| Architecture leads to real source | Mapped-file filtering/refresh, safe paths, actual editor open/save/return |
| Native diagram remains readable and interactive | Flat/nested views, node/group clicks, projected markers, narrow/wide inspector checks |
| Live activity is truthful | Real journal events, project/session isolation, no camera movement or synthetic connection traffic |
| Integration is safe | Usable-frame readiness, pane reuse/replacement, error rollback, signal and editor-group cleanup |
| The approved experience survives implementation changes | Terminal regression checks plus an actual visual check when appearance or movement changes |

Automated tests establish behavior, not universal visual quality or portability.
Keep platform-specific and manual verification claims separate.

## Non-goals for the current scope

- Replacing LikeC4 with an inferred architecture model or automatic layout system.
- Inferring file ownership, links, runtime traffic or test outcomes from agent prose.
- Editing the architecture model through the viewer, or becoming a source editor.
- A hosted dashboard, network telemetry service, collaborative presence system,
  or durable audit log.
- Automatically recording every agent/subagent session, or presenting a subagent's work as the conversation's own. Claude subagent calls are recorded with their type as a label and can be hidden; they are never unlabeled.
- Pixel-identical reproduction of every LikeC4 shape in native terminal cells.

These are scope boundaries, not promises of later implementation.

## Current limits and remaining validation

- Linux/tmux is verified. macOS and broader terminal compatibility remain open;
  locking is a plain lockfile, so it is not Linux-specific, but nothing has been run on macOS. A compiled single binary works on Linux x64 only so far.
- Connectors are routed by a simple grid search; in very dense diagrams two routes can share a lane or pass close to a node.
- Labels may clip or hide at small scales; boxes move on terminal-cell boundaries.
  Dot and diamond markers are drawn as plain arrowheads.
- Group collapsing, relationship-link navigation and model editing are not
  implemented. Search covers every view, box and mapped file, but only those
  the model and mapping give it: unmapped or ignored files are not searchable.
- Journals can lose events under overload or disk failure. Their bounded history
  cannot answer historical questions like a durable event store.

Near-term work should harden and validate this working loop, address concrete
usability failures, and improve compatibility without sacrificing the approved
camera or inventing observation semantics. New product capabilities should be
proposed against this intent before expanding the scope.

# Quick start

Pathlight draws your codebase's architecture beside your AI coding agent and lights up the parts it reads and edits. This page is the one screen you need; [the viewer reference](native-viewer.md) has the rest.

## Open it

In a tmux pane, in the project you work in:

- **Claude Code** (with the plugin): type `/pathlight:map`. The first time, the agent runs `pathlight setup`, draws a first map from the code, names its boxes, shows the first-day briefing (`pathlight brief --first-day`: what it is, how it is built, where it starts, the journeys, how sure the names are), and opens the viewer beside the conversation. Say "walk me through this codebase" and it follows the journeys step by step, moving the diagram to each box once you agree. Later, `/pathlight:open` reopens it without asking the model.
- **OpenCode** (with the plugin): type `/pathlight`, and `/pathlight-open` to reopen it.
- **A shell**: `pathlight setup --yes` draws the map, `pathlight init --workspace .` wires the agent's hooks, `pathlight open` turns the pane into the viewer.

## Three keys to start

- A click or `h j k l` selects a box; the inspector on the right says what it is and what it connects to, and `tab` goes into it, card by card.
- `t` asks the agent about it. On first open the question is already there (`how does … work?`): press Enter, and the answer arrives in chat and is drawn on the map.
- `F` steps through what was drawn, one hop at a time (`[` `]` move, `esc` leaves).

`?` lists every key, in three groups, in the order you will want them.

## Understand it

Everyone starts here, even on their own code. Select boxes (a click, `h j k l`), go into a group with `enter`, and step back with `backspace` (or `b`): back where you were, else up a level. Ask how something works with `t`: a question about a path ("how does a document get saved?", "where does the token go?") is answered and recorded as a journey, which `F` walks on the diagram. Everything drawn this way is the agent's reading of the code, in violet, never something observed.

## Direct it

Once you know the ground, the same `t` tells the agent what to change ("add a health-check route"). Before it edits a file it declares where it will work: the boxes it will touch are outlined, and anything new appears dashed where you pointed. As it works, the boxes it reads and edits light up; `a` follows the work, `w` jumps to it, `c` shows the session and asks you about any new dependency the code gained. `e` lists a box's files and opens one in your editor, `/` searches, `g` changes view, `b` goes back, `f` fits.

## Shape the map

The map is yours to correct. `d` asks the agent to trace a flow from the selected box, `m` asks it to improve a box's name and description, `n` lets you write them yourself (yours are never overwritten). `p` replays the session, `s` hides subagent calls, `T` picks a theme.

## What it is not

Pathlight shows the code's structure (from its imports), the agent's reading of it, and the tool calls the agent made. It never shows runtime traffic, and it says which of the three each thing on screen is. Linux and tmux are the verified platform.

# Scan format

`pathlight scan [--workspace PATH] [--out FILE]` reads a workspace's TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go and Rust source and writes one JSON document. It exists so that an agent drafting a LikeC4 model does not have to read the whole codebase, and so the same facts can feed several views. It does not write or change a model.

Everything in it is a **static** reading of source text (`"basis": "static"`). It says what the code names, not what runs: a dynamic `import(name)`, a bundler alias or a framework convention is invisible to it, and an import is not proof of a call.

## What it contains

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `root` | The workspace directory's name (no absolute paths, no dates: scanning the same tree twice gives the same text). |
| `files` | Every scanned file: `path`, `language` (`typescript`, `javascript`, `python`, `go`, `rust`), `lines`, and the names it `exports` (at most 80). |
| `imports` | Imports that resolve to a file in the workspace: `from`, `to`, the `line` where the statement starts, its `kind`, the original `specifier`, and `uses`: how `from` uses each name it takes from `to` (below). |
| `external` | Packages outside the workspace (and `node:`/`bun:` built-ins), once per importing file. |
| `unresolved` | Imports that look like they point into the workspace but did not resolve, each with a `reason`: `not-found`, `alias-not-configured` or `package-entry-not-found`. Workspace-package imports follow the target package's `exports` map the same way, including `*` patterns (an explicit entry wins over a pattern). `#name` imports are Node subpath imports: the scan follows the nearest `package.json` `imports` field (resolved with [resolve.exports](https://github.com/lukeed/resolve.exports)) to every runtime variant it names (`bun`, `node`, `workerd`, `default`...), since a static scan cannot know which runtime applies; one that maps to nothing is `alias-not-configured`. |
| `coverage` | How the files were listed (`git` or `walk`), counts, how many files were `skipped`, and `unscanned` languages that are present but not read. |

`kind` is `import`, `type` (an `import type`, `export type … from`, or an import whose every binding is `type`; in Python, an import under `if TYPE_CHECKING:`), `reexport`, `dynamic` (`import("x")` with a literal; in Python, `importlib.import_module("a.b")` or `__import__("a.b")`) or `require`.

## Uses

Each import record lists how the importing file uses what it takes from the target, read from the syntax alone, the strongest use of each name first, at most 12: `[{ "name": "createDocument", "how": "calls" }, { "name": "User", "how": "types" }]`. A module imported whole (`import * as api`, Python `import app.mail`, a Go package) lists the members used through it (`api.createDocument(…)` is `createDocument`).

| `how` | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `calls` | `f(…)`, `X.method(…)`, a Go `pkg.Func(…)`, a Rust `path::f(…)` or `Type::method(…)`, a macro, a decorator. A member called through a parameter, field or variable annotated with the imported type (`(db: Db) => db.query()`, Go `func f(s *store.Store) { s.Get() }`, Rust `fn f(c: &Client) { c.send() }`) is a call of that type (`Db.query`), since the file runs that type's code. Methods every value has (`clone`, `toString`, `iter`, `map` …) do not count, and neither does an annotation that is a collection of the type (`Db[]`, `[]*Store`, `Vec<Client>`). |
| `renders` | A JSX element (`<Button />`). |
| `constructs` | `new X(…)`, a Go composite literal `pkg.T{…}`, a Rust struct literal. |
| `extends` | A class's base, Python `class A(Base)`, an embedded Go struct, a Rust `impl Trait for`. |
| `references` | Used as a value any other way: passed, stored, compared, spread, exported again. A position the reading cannot place counts here, so a doubt keeps an arrow. |
| `types` | Only in type positions: annotations, signatures, generic arguments, `implements`, `type` and `interface` bodies, `as`. |

An import **carries code** unless every use it lists is `types` (or, with no uses read, it is written as a type import). An import with no uses read (a side-effect import, `require`, a dynamic import, a name never used) carries code: nothing says it does not. The draft draws an arrow only where an import carries code (`docs/eval.md`, "Uses"); `check` does not ask for one that only shares types; a journey step that names a function is checked against these uses.

What is not seen: a member called on a value whose type the file never writes (an inferred type), a type named only in a string annotation (Python `"Repo"`), and calls through a field reached by more than one dot. TypeScript is read from the tokenizer (template expressions and JSX tag names included; JSX text and attribute names are not code), Python, Go and Rust from their syntax trees. The reading is measured against TypeScript's own compiler and Go's type checker (`tests/eval/facts-uses.ts`).

## Languages

Each language is read by a front end in `src/languages/` that gives the rest of the scan the same records, so the draft, `check`, `diff`, `brief`, flows and the viewer read every language alike. TypeScript and JavaScript are read by the hand-written tokenizer in `src/scan-imports.ts`; Python, Go and Rust by tree-sitter grammars compiled into the binary (nothing is downloaded, and a grammar is loaded only when the workspace has a file in its language).

| Language | Statements read | Resolved by | Not followed (listed, never guessed) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TypeScript, JavaScript (`.ts .tsx .mts .cts .js .jsx .mjs .cjs`) | `import`, `export … from`, `import()` and `require()` with a literal | Relative paths, the nearest tsconfig `baseUrl`/`paths`, workspace packages through `exports`/`main`, `#` subpath imports; a name is followed through barrels (below) | `extends` chains, bundler and framework aliases |
| Python (`.py`) | `import a.b`, `from a.b import c`, relative `from . import x` / `from ..a import y`, `from a import *`, anywhere in a file; `importlib.import_module`/`__import__` with a literal | Roots: the folder of each `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py` and `setup.cfg`, its `src/`, a folder its `package-dir` (`package_dir`, Poetry's `from`) names, and the workspace root; the nearest root above a file first. `a.b.c` is `a/b/c.py` or `a/b/c/__init__.py`; `from a.b import c` is the module `c` if there is one, else the name `c` in `a/b`. A folder without `__init__.py` is a namespace package. A name taken from a package is followed through its `__init__.py`'s `from .mod import name` (and `*`) to the module that defines it. A first segment that is no package of the workspace is a package from outside | `sys.path` edits (including in `conftest.py`), `PYTHONPATH`, `.pth` files, names built at run time |
| Go (`.go`) | every `import` | The nearest `go.mod` names a file's module; a nested `go.mod` is its own module; `go.work` lists modules; a `replace` to a local path is followed; `vendor/` is not read. An import is recorded against the files of the package that declare the names the importing file uses (`storage.New`, `storage.Entry`); a dot or blank import, or a used name no file declares, reaches every file of the package. Test files are read as sources and never targets. The standard library and other modules are packages from outside | Build constraints (`//go:build`, `_linux.go`): every file is read whatever its tags; cgo |
| Rust (`.rs`) | every `use` (groups, `as`, globs, `pub use`), `extern crate`, and a path written in code or a type whose first segment is `crate`, `self`, `super`, `::`, a name a `use` brought in, or a crate (`atuin_common::utils::now()`); code under `#[cfg(test)]` is a test and is not read | Each `Cargo.toml` with a `[package]` is a crate, its targets found as Cargo finds them (`src/lib.rs`, `src/main.rs`, `src/bin/`, the build script, `examples/`, `tests/`, `benches/`, and `[lib]`, `[[bin]]` and the rest); dependencies through `workspace = true` and `package = "…"` renames, a path dependency to that crate's library. From each target's root, `mod x;` is `x.rs` or `x/mod.rs` beside a `lib.rs`, `main.rs` or `mod.rs` and under `a/` for `a.rs`; `#[path]` and inline modules are followed. A path resolves module by module; the segment after the last module is the name taken from that module's file, followed through `pub use` (and `pub use …::*`) like a barrel. Edition 2015 `use` paths start at the crate root. `vendor/` is not read. A crate from outside is named with the next segment of its path (`sqlx/sqlite`); `std`, `core` and `alloc` by name. A file no `mod` reaches is read where it sits under `src/` | `mod x;` (where a file sits, not a use of it); any other `cfg` (features, platforms): every module is read; macros called by bare name; methods and fields (they need types); `include!`; paths inside macro arguments |

## What it follows

- Relative imports, including `.js` specifiers that name a `.ts` file, directory indexes, and non-source files such as `.css` and `.json`.
- The nearest `tsconfig.json`/`jsconfig.json` `baseUrl` and `paths` (comments and trailing commas allowed).
- Packages with a `package.json` inside the workspace (monorepo packages), through `exports`, `main`, `module` and `types`; an entry that names built output (`dist/…`) is looked up under `src/…`.
- Re-exports. A package's entry file usually declares nothing and re-exports everything, so an import of it only says which barrel was named. Each name an import takes is followed through `export * from`, `export { a as b } from` and their `type` forms (and nested barrels) to the file that declares it, and the import is recorded against that file, one record per file reached (same `line` and `specifier`). A namespace import (`import * as`), a side-effect import, or a name that cannot be followed stays on the file it named. The barrel's own `export … from` lines are kept as they are.

It does not follow `extends` chains, bundler or framework aliases, or anything built at run time. What that leaves behind is in `unresolved` or `coverage.unscanned`, not guessed.

Files come from `git ls-files` (tracked plus untracked, ignoring what `.gitignore` excludes) or, outside a repository, a walk that skips `.git`, `.cache` and `node_modules`. Symlinks and files over 2 MiB are skipped and counted. A workspace listing more than 50,000 files is refused; scan a subdirectory.

## How it was checked

The import reader is compared in the tests with Bun's own scanner on this repository's value imports (they agree), and it additionally reports type-only imports and line numbers, which Bun's does not. Run against three real repositories, it found every relative import that an independent regular-expression scan found.

Uses are compared with the compilers' own answers (`tests/eval/facts-uses.ts`): for TypeScript, which import bindings `tsc` removes when it emits JavaScript (a binding no value position uses), and for Go, `go/types` on whether each use of a package sits in a type position; see [eval](eval.md#uses-2026-11-10). Python and Go are compared with each language's own tools: CPython's `ast` and `importlib.machinery.PathFinder` for Python (`tests/eval/facts-python.ts`), `go list` for Go at the package level (`tests/eval/facts-go.ts`); see [eval](eval.md#languages-2026-10-28). Rust is compared with `cargo metadata` at the crate level and rust-analyzer's SCIP index at the file level (`tests/eval/facts-rust.ts`); see [eval](eval.md#rust-2026-11-10).

# Check

`pathlight check [--workspace PATH] [--json] [--strict]` compares a workspace's LikeC4 model and `.pathlight/pathlight.activity.json` with a fresh scan. It is the validator for a model an agent drafted from the scan, and it catches drift when the code changes and the model does not. Like the scan, everything in it is static evidence: a finding is something to look at, not a verdict.

An element's files are those its mappings match; for a relationship, the files of everything *inside* an element count too, so a relationship on a group is supported by imports between its children's files.

| Section | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `mappings.shared`, `mappings.sharedImports` | The elements `shared` names in `.pathlight/pathlight.activity.json` (anything may import them, so no relationship is expected) and how many imports into them were left out of `undeclared`. |
| `size` | Files per element, largest first. An element with at least 15 files and a quarter or more of all mapped files is `large`, with the folders inside it. A hint that it may be several things, not a verdict. |
| `wide` | Elements with more than 19 cards side by side inside them (the cards their own readable view draws, else their direct children), the most the draft draws in one box. A hint to group them. |
| `views` | `entries` are the written views no `navigateTo` points to. A diagram normally has one, so more than one is reported as `unlinkedViews`. LikeC4's generated Landscape index is not counted. |
| `mappings.ignored` | Source files left out of "unmapped" by the optional `ignore` list in `.pathlight/pathlight.activity.json` (globs for tests, vendored or generated code that is deliberately outside the model). Only `check` reads it; activity mapping is unchanged. |
| `mappings.unmatched` | A mapping whose glob matches no file in the workspace. |
| `mappings.unmappedFiles` | Scanned source files that no mapping claims, so activity on them lights nothing. |
| `relationships` | Each relationship in the model with a `status`: `supported` (an import connects the two elements' files), `unsupported` (none does) or `unverifiable` (an end has no mapped files). |
| `undeclared` | Imports between two mapped elements that no relationship declares, at that level or above, in either direction. |

A relationship describes flow or use, while an import points from the user to what it uses, so either direction supports a relationship; `direction` says whether the imports run `same` as the relationship, `opposite`, or `both`. `unsupported` does not mean the relationship is wrong: it may run through a network call, an event, a file or configuration, none of which an import shows. An unknown element in a mapping is an error, not a finding. `--strict` makes any finding (an unmatched glob, an unmapped file, an unsupported relationship, an undeclared import) exit 1; unverifiable relationships do not.

name: pathlight-namer
description: Names and describes every box of a pathlight map so the diagram is understandable on first opening (pathlight brief, then pathlight name). Use after pathlight setup has drawn a first map, when asked to name or explain the boxes, or for a whole package at once. Runs on a mid-size model so a large conversation model does not spend its tokens reading code.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: sonnet
---

You give the boxes of a pathlight map a plain name and a one-sentence note that says what each is for. You are given a workspace, and optionally the keys of the boxes to cover; with none, cover all of them. Do only that.

1. Get the facts: `pathlight brief --workspace .` (or `pathlight brief KEY ... --workspace .` for part of the map). Each box lists the files it owns with their sizes, what it imports from, what imports it, what is inside it and any name it already has. Boxes come children first, so you can name a parent from what is inside it. When the map was named before and the code has moved on, `pathlight brief --changed --workspace .` lists only the boxes that are new or whose files changed since `pathlight name` recorded them (never one a person named); cover just those. A big map: take it a package at a time.
2. Work out what each box is for. The files listed are the box: a folder plus a loose file beside it is one box, so describe all of it, not the one folder you happened to open. Open the files that decide it (the entry point, the biggest file, a README or a header comment); do not name a box from its folder name alone. What a box *is for in this app* matters more than what it contains: "Checks a login before any page loads", not "Auth utilities".
   A box whose description says "not read by the scan" is code in another language (Go, Zig, Python…): the brief lists no imports for it because the scan cannot read them, not because there are none. Open its files to name it, and if you saw how the rest of the code reaches it (a binding file, FFI, a subprocess, HTTP), say so in the note.
3. Say how sure you are. A note for a box whose files you did not open with Read ends with "(inferred from file names)", inside the 300 characters, because the briefing counts every note without it as read from the code; a skim of the brief's file list is not reading. A box you cannot tell the purpose of gets an honest note, not a plausible one. Never describe behavior you did not see in code.
   With no keys the brief also lists “Where the code can be started”: scripts, bins and main files the project declares, and files no other file imports, each with its box. They are facts about where to begin, not what the app does; read them before suggesting journeys.
   With no keys, the brief opens with “About the project”: the package description, the start of the README and the documents the project keeps. Use it for the box that holds the whole app (the package or top-level box, often key `.`): its note says what the app is for and who it serves, in the project's own terms, not how its folders are laid out. Name that box last, once you have read the boxes inside it. Do not repeat the README's wording where the code says otherwise, and say so in the note when it does.
4. Write them in batches, one level at a time (children first), with one command per batch:
   `pathlight name --workspace . --from - <<< '[{"key": "...", "title": "...", "note": "..."},{...}]'`, the whole JSON array on one line, an apostrophe inside it written `'\''`, never a heredoc, because a heredoc holding JSON is refused under the `Bash(pathlight *)` rule that `pathlight init` writes. The key is exactly the box's key from the brief. A title is at most 60 characters, a note at most 300, one line each, plain words. Use `--note` or `--title` alone only to change one of them.
5. If the command says it kept a name, a person wrote it: leave it. If it says a key matches no box, fix the key from the brief.

Rules: read-only except for `pathlight name`. Do not change product code, the model, or the mapping, and do not run the viewer. Read and search files with the Read, Grep and Glob tools, not the shell. Use the shell only for `pathlight` commands and `git log`, `git show` or `ls`: some hosts refuse anything else, and a refused command does not mean the `pathlight` one will be refused, so still run it.

When you were given keys because Pathlight drew new boxes at the end of a turn, cover only those, then reply with one line per box (`key: title`) and the boxes you could not tell, and stop: no briefing, no journeys.

Otherwise, when the last batch is saved, run `pathlight brief --first-day --workspace .`: the briefing a person new to the code reads first, made from the scan and the names you just saved. Reply in this shape and nothing else:

1. The briefing, exactly as the command printed it: do not summarise, reorder or add to it.
2. Up to three journeys worth tracing as flows, each as one line naming the file it starts at and what the person sees (for example “src/main.ts: a message typed in the chat window goes through the pipeline and the reply comes back”). Choose journeys that start at a start the briefing lists and the app really uses, not a test or a one-off script. They are suggestions from what you read; do not trace or record them yourself.
3. What you could not tell: any box whose purpose you could not tell, with what you saw, and anything the command kept or refused. Say "nothing" when there is nothing.

description: Traces how something works through the components of a codebase and records it as a pathlight journey (pathlight flow add). Use when asked to trace, draw or record a flow, including the request the pathlight viewer's `t` or `d` key sends. Runs on a mid-size model so a large conversation model does not spend its tokens reading code.

You trace one path through a codebase and record it as a pathlight journey. You are given a request naming a component, a question to trace, and the component's files and connections. Do only that.

These are the pathlight behavior skill's steps for a journey, complete; you do not need to look for the skill.

1. Find the components: `pathlight list --workspace .` and the LikeC4 model give the ids; `.pathlight/pathlight.activity.json` maps files to them.
2. Start at the entry point the question names and follow the code outward. Open the files. For each hop you will use, you must be able to point to the file and line where one component calls or hands off to the next.
3. Drop any hop you cannot point to. Do not guess, and do not fill a gap to make the picture complete.
4. Record it with one command, using the ids exactly as the model spells them and the files you actually read:
   `pathlight flow add ID --workspace . --title 'TITLE' --reads FILE,FILE --step 'FROM -> TO: what happens' ...`
   When a hop is a call to an exported function, say which: end the step with ` @ path/file.ts#functionName` (the file must be one you read and must export that name; the command refuses anything else and copies the declaration from the file). Name the function that does the step (the handler that receives the request, the one that polls), not the one that only creates the object doing it, and give one for every hop you can; leave it off only when you cannot point to the function.
   Add `--project NAME` if the repository has several LikeC4 projects. Use a short lowercase id such as `place-order`.
   When a hop goes over HTTP, a websocket or a spawned process rather than an import, write it `--step 'FROM -> TO over http: what happens'` (`over websocket`, `over process`). Do that only when you have read both the file and line that make the request (the fetch, the socket send, the spawn) and the file that answers it (the route, the handler, the program run); otherwise leave `over` off.
5. If the command reports a hop with no arrow on the map (no relationship in the model), leave it and say which you think is wrong, the story or the model. A step back along the way an earlier step went is read as that step's answer and is not reported. Never edit the model, and never add `over`, to silence it.

Rules: read-only except for the one `pathlight flow add` command. Do not change product code. Do not run the viewer. Read and search files with the Read, Grep and Glob tools, not the shell. Use the shell only for `pathlight` commands and `git log`, `git show` or `ls`: some hosts refuse anything else, and a refused command does not mean the `pathlight` one will be refused, so still run it.

Reply in this shape and nothing else:

- The exact `pathlight flow add` command you ran, and its output.
- What each hop rests on (file and function).
- What you could not find or left out, and anything the command flagged.
